title: Bonn / Dusseldorf - 1980
text: Bonn / Dusseldorf - 1980 Bonn / Düsseldorf - September 1980 I'd come to Bonn to stay with Gregor König whom I had met the year before at a Kate Bush concert in London, when she played at the London Palladium and, later, at the Hammersmith Odeon. He was a budding music journalist. There wasn't a huge amount to do in Bonn: it enjoyed a reputation as a city of administration and bureaucracy. We drove to Düsseldorf one day as Gregor was to interview German 'punk' singer Nina Hagen. I met her but she completely ignored me ... After this we toured the town and visited the local park where we saw a monument to composer Robert Schumann. The reason for my visit was because Gregor had free tickets to a Udo Lindenberg concert. Most people in the UK have never heard of him but he was a huge star in Germany and regularly sold-out large concert halls and arenas. He was also prominent in the Rock gegen Rechts movement (concerts and festivals held irregularly against far-right politics as a form of political demonstration). Udo Lindenberg called his events Rock gegen rechte Gewalt (Rock against far-right violence). At the concert I was surprised / delighted to meet avant garde artist Joseph Beuys who signed my ticket stub. His extensive work is grounded in concepts of humanism and social philosophy; it culminates in his "extended definition of art" and the idea of social sculpture as a gesamtkunstwerk . He is widely regarded as one of the most influential artists of the second half of the 20th century. There was a Beuys exhibition taking place in Düsseldorf at the time which I visited. Richtkrafte / Directional Forces (1974–77) Tisch mit Aggregat / Table with Aggregator (1958–85) and Three Pots for the Poorhouse (1974) Das Rudel / The Pack (1969) The previous year in London, I had taken Gregor to Notting Hill and to Camden market - and back to my student accommodation for tea (how English!).

title: Brussels - 2001
text: Brussels - 2001 Brussels - October 2001 A surprise 50th birthday treat for Seán's sister, Marie. We took the Eurostar train to Brussels and met her as she came through the turnstiles at Brussels station and then whisked her off for a gourmet lunch. First of all however we stopped off at the Atomium - a landmark building, originally constructed for the 1958 Brussels World’s Fair (Expo 58). Now a museum, it was designed by the engineer André Waterkeyn and architects André and Jean Polak and stands 335 feet tall. Its nine stainless steel clad spheres are connected in the shape of a unit cell that could represent an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times. Tubes connecting the spheres enclose stairs, escalators and an elevator (in the central, vertical tube) to allow access to the five habitable spheres, which contain exhibit halls and other public spaces. The top sphere includes a restaurant which has a panoramic view of Brussels.

title: Budapest - 2005
text: Budapest - 2005 Budapest - February 2005 A trip to Hungary to visit my American friend Tom Rooney (with whom I stayed in San Francisco back in 1991). Tom had moved to Hungary to do his Peace Corps volunteering and had met and married György, an English teacher who specialised in the works of Jane Austen. Hösök tere (Heroes' Square) is one of the major sites in Budapest, noted for its iconic statue complex featuring the Seven chieftains of the Magyars and other Hungarian national leaders, as well as the Memorial Stone of Heroes. We then walked across the Chain Bridge, one of Budapest's important river crossings across the Danube. Posing in front of the River Danube . On our trip on the Budapest metro we were amused to see the Hungarian poster for Wesley Snipes' film Blade: Trilogy ... The Hotel Gellért features the famous bath complex which was built between 1912-1918 in the (Secession) Art Nouveau style. References to healing waters in this location are found from as early as the 13th century. A hospital was located on this site during the Middle Ages. During the reign of the Ottoman Empire, baths were also built on this site. The "magical healing spring" was used by the Turkish during the 16th and 17th centuries. The bath was called Sárosfürdö ("muddy" bath) because the mineral mud settled at the bottom of pools. The Gellért Baths feature elaborately-tiled steam rooms and plunge pools - as well as a covered swimming pool. We decided to "take the plunge" (well, it would be churlish not to) and found the water deliciously warm. After having our swim, we climbed the nearby Gellért Hill through the snow to see the statue of Szent Gellért (St. Gerard) who was a bishop canonised after his assassination by pagans during the great pagan rebellion in 1046. He was put in a barrel and thrown from the top of the hill. On our final evening, we met Tom and György again who took us to a 'typically Hungarian' restaurant but the food, I must admit, I cannot now remember. St. Stephen’s Basilica is a Roman Catholic church named in honour of Stephen, the first King of Hungary (c.975-1038), whose right hand is housed in the reliquary. We only saw it by night so missed the hand.

title: Cordoba - 2013
text: Cordoba - 2013 Córdoba - September 2013 One of the first things you see on arriving in Córdoba is the Roman Bridge over the Guadalquivir River which links the area of Campo de la Verdad with Barrio de la Catedral . Built in the early 1st century BC, it was the only bridge in the city for twenty centuries. During the 18th century, numerous statues of The Triumph of Saint Raphael the Archangel were erected to protect the city against the plaque. Of the eight “triumphs” that remain in Córdoba, the most majestic was sculpted by Miguel de Verdiguer and erected near the Roman Bridge in 1765. The most iconic building in Córdoba is the Mezquita . It was built as an Islamic mosque but, before that, the site was host to a Visigothic church, the Catholic Christian Basilica of Saint Vincent of Saragossa. The current building was originally constructed on the orders of Abd al-Rahman I in 785 AD, when Córdoba was the capital of the Muslim-controlled region of Al-Andalus. The mosque was converted to a cathedral in 1236 when Córdoba was captured by the Christian forces of Castile during the Reconquista. It has many notable metal exterior doors which add lustre to an already mesmerising building. The Mezquita's Hypostyle hall dates from the original mosque construction and originally served as its main prayer space for Muslims. It also would have served as a hall for teaching and for Sharia law cases during the rule of Abd al-Rahman and his successors. The famous alternating red and white horseshoe arches were inspired by those in the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem and also resemble those of Aachen Cathedral, which were built almost at the same time. There is a museum incorporated into the Mezquita ( Museo de San Clemente ) which features all sorts of religious knick-knackery which I love, including a Roman Missal which was published in Antwerp in 1634. It is an astonishing building with its crazy mix of Islamic and high Gothic architecture. The Alcázar de los Reyes Cristianos (Castle of the Christian Monarchs) is located in the historic centre of Córdoba near the Grand Mosque. The fortress served as one of the primary residences of Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon. Its construction was ordered by King Alfonso XI of Castile in 1328, on previous constructions (the Islamic-era Umayyad Alcázar, also the previous residence of the Roman Governor and the Customs). It later served as home to the first permanent tribunal of the Spanish Inquisition and as a headquarters for their campaign against the Nasrid dynasty in Granada, the last remaining Moorish kingdom in the Iberian Peninsula. The Inquisition began using the Alcázar as one of its headquarters in 1482, converting much of it, including the Arab baths, into torture and interrogation chambers. The Inquisition maintained a tribunal here for three centuries. Gardens have existed at the Alcázar since the 10th century when Abd al-Rahman III constructed an aquaduct to bring water from the nearby Albolafia waterwheel. The gardens have been neglected or renewed at various times since then. In the late 15th century Queen Isabella I ordered the waterwheel's operation to be halted, and they went into a general decline. Today the gardens consist of an impressive area of approximately 55,000m² of magnificent gardens with forest species including palm, cypress, orange and lemon trees, which surround a number of elegant fountains and ponds. The Lower Garden also includes the Paseo de los Reyes (King's Avenue or Promenade of Kings), an avenue bordered by lines of cylindrical cypress trees and divided into two paths by two narrow ponds. On this walk, there are several sculptures of the Kings who built the Alcázar, which are located on pedestals aligned between the hedges. The journey back to Mijas was hot and the roads were fairly punishing, so we stopped for refreshment at a service station and enjoyed a coffee and flan - Andalusia's version of crème caramel.

title: Croatia - 2014
text: Croatia - 2014 Croatia - June 2014 We had been invited to go on a chartered yacht trip round the Croatian islands by Seán's friends Geraldine and Niall along with their pals Bernadette "Ber", husband Paul and friend Catherine - something we had never done before - so we jumped at the chance. We flew out to Split and then took a taxi to Tisno on the island of Murter for an overnight at a very pretty hotel. The next day the Irish contingent arrived ... High-heeled shoes had to be removed before the girls could board the boat. Once the luggage was aboard, we could all settle down with a refreshing G & T. We set off from Jezera on the island of Murter - with our experienced captain at the helm. He didn't speak much English and we spoke absolutely NO Croatian, but we seemed to understand each other. Passing under the Sibenik Bridge , we took the opportunity for our first swim. We moored at Skradin for our first night - in the same spot where the original Roman port was situated. It is also the location where the Krka River flows into the sea. A storm had been forecast overnight and we were glad we were in a sheltered mooring at Skradin . Indeed the dinghy which was left on deck was blown overboard and had to be retrieved from the other end of the marina. After another day's sailing, we arrived for the next mooring at Milna on the Island of Brac . This spot is the home of a quarry, famous for the white-as-snow Brac stone which was used in the building of Diocletian's Palace in Split and was also used in part of the White House in Washington. The next morning found another beautiful day - and we set off for the Island of Hvar . While the idea of sailing round the Adriatic sounds luxurious, the reality below deck was of cramped conditions and airless space. Our 'cabin' had a vent in the ceiling but this was always blocked because the onboard safety dinghy was stored on deck right above where the vent should open. Toilets too were cramped and we had to adopt a "liquids only" rule on board to keep it pleasant for everyone ... Here we all are ready to go out to supper at Hvar . The marina was at Vrboska, nearby to a rare fortified church from the 16th century - the only one of its kind in Dalmatia. We had to take a speed boat from the marina into the town of Hvar which was on the other side of the island. We found a wonderful rooftop restaurant for supper. Hvar was a real party town - loud throbbing music pulsed from all the bars on the sea front - so we were lucky to find a relative oasis of calm 'up on the roof'. The next day was Ber's 50th birthday - and we had a good excuse to start the day with some rosé fizz ... We had a long day's sailing ahead of us - but we stopped off for lunch at a delightful spot. Even our captain wanted to take a dip. More sailing after lunch and we arrived into Trogir - a truly magnificent medieval town where, after the girls stopped at a hairdressers for a blow-dry and the boys for a beer or two, we went out for the big birthday supper. Another day of sailing and we arrived in Primosten , a pretty little town in North Dalmatia, which was once on an island (as could be told from its shape), although it was linked to the mainland in the 16th century. We had supper there but we all had to move tables twice as Ber was spooked by some cats who happened to live at the restaurant. Our faces show what we were thinking ... The next day we returned to Murter and, like when you hire a car, we had to fill up the boat with fuel before it went back to the marina. Note the extremely long hose from the pump to the boat which moored right up beside the petrol station. We then said a sad farewell to the Irish mob who were directly flying home. Seán and I had booked another day or so in Split as this was a town we wished to explore. The bougainvillea was in full bloom when we arrived. The major tourist attraction in Split was Diocletian's Palace - a heavily fortified compound near the Roman Emperor's hometown of Spalatum in preparation for his retirement in May 305 AD. We spent our final afternoon walking round the rather splendid town before our flight home the next day.

title: Croatia 2015
text: Croatia - 2015 Croatia - June 2015 We returned to Trogir in 2015 after our visit the year before as we found it a magical place and worthy of further exploration. The Cathedral of St. Lawrence is a Roman Catholic triple-naved basilica constructed in Romanesque-Gothic. Construction lasted several centuries, so it illustrates many of the styles that succeeded one another in Dalmatia. It serves now as the most imposing monument in the city of Trogir. It was built on the foundations of an Early Christian cathedral destroyed in the 12th century during the sack of Trogir by the Saracens in 1123. The building of the cathedral began in 1213 and finished during the 17th century. Most of the work in the construction of the cathedral took place in the 13th century, being largely completed in 1251. This means the building is mainly in Romanesque style, whilst the vault inside is gothic as it was built during the 15th century, in Mannerist style. Work on the bell tower began at the end of the 14th century, but it was not completed until the end of the 16th century. The first floor is in Gothic style and was built by Masters Stejpan and Matej. After it had been demolished by the Venetians in 1420, it was restored by Matija Gojkovic. The local architect and sculptor Master Radovan worked on the cathedral's gateway (main west portal) early in its construction. Finished and signed in 1240, it is a monumental and perhaps unique work of this great Croatian artist, of whom the inscription on the base of the lunette says: " the best of all in this artisanship ". We toured the island in our hire car and found a beautiful but deserted beach with crystal clear water and a heavenly view. Naturally I had to take a dip (but no photo was taken) ... The back alleyways and passages of Trogir were unexpectedly filled with flowers - hollyhocks and oleanders were really pretty. We ate well too - returning to several restaurants we had visited the previous year - and enjoying the delicious cold Malvasia wine. We took the car one day to the ancient town of Salona which is only 5km from Split and is famous for its Roman ruins. The name Salona (or Salonae) derives from the salt works ( sal in Latin) in the area. Then a boat trip from Trogir into Split - where we explored Diocletian's Palace and bought a hat each. In the harbour was a sister ship to the Costa Concordia , the ship which grounded and sank off the coast of Isola del Giglio, resulting in the deaths of 33 people. They were monsters of vessels and very ugly. Then back to Trogir for our final night there and a visit to our favourite restaurant before leaving for Tisno the following morning. NEXT

title: Croatia
text: Croatia Croatia - June 2014 Croatia - June 2015

title: Croatia2 2015
text: Croatia - 2015 Croatia - June 2015 It was lovely to come back to Tisno on the island of Murter. This time we had a small suite at the front of the Hotel Tisno which overlooked the harbour - heavenly! As well as the hats which we purchased in Split, we also needed some footwear for the beach and these lovely ladies had just set up shop for the season - where we bought deck shoes and Croatian stripy T-shirts. As a 'thank you' for our custom, they also gave us a mug. Krka National Park is named after the River Krka (ancient Greek: Kyrikos ) and is located along the middle course of the river in central Dalmatia, in Šibenik-Knin county, just a few kilometres northeast of the city of Šibenik. Skradinski buk is one of the most attractive parts of the park. It is a massive, clear, natural pool with high waterfalls at one end and cascades at the other. It is the lowest of the three sets of waterfalls formed along the River Krka. Due to the variety of geomorphological forms, vegetation and the various effects caused by the play of light on the whirlpools, Skradinski buk is considered to be one of the most beautiful calcium carbonate waterfalls in Europe. We then took a boat out onto Lake Visovac to visit the Monastery of Visovac which was founded by Franciscan monks in 1445 and then joined by Franciscans from Bosnia in 1576. We returned to Tisno in time to take part in the annual gastronomic festival - of biza i boba (peas and beans) - where villagers set up makeshift stalls serving pulse-based soups, stews and pasta sauces. All were surprisingly delicious. As with many of these events, the evening was rounded off by a rather duff band belting out favourite local tunes. We didn't buy the CD ... We ate well at Tisno tavernas - returning to our preferred restaurant from the previous year. The anchovy and rocket salad was particularly delicious. As we had a boat back in Kingsbridge we felt bold enough to hire a boat and tour the island of Murter from the sea. It was great fun - but blazing hot and we were relieved to have a canopy to shelter us from the sun. Coming back into Tisno harbour we had to disassemble the canopy to allow the boat to get under the road bridge - a rather nerve-wracking experience. We passed our hotel (above left) while in the boat and continued and moored up at a particularly beautiful spot and had another swim. The next day we took the car north to the port of Zadar, passing some interesting restaurants along the road where they roasted their own suckling pigs in giant ovens. In the Middle Ages Zadar was the main base for the Byzantine fleet. Venice and the King of Hungary fought over Zadar in the 12th and 13th centuries but, in 1409, King Ladislaus of Hungary sold his Dalmatian islands and cities to Venice for 100,000 ducats. Around the sea border of Zadar are several interesting and unusual features. The Greeting to the Sun (above) is a remarkable installation made out of 300 photo-sensitive glass plates that absorb daylight and transform into a wondrous light show at night. The Sea Organ (Croatian: Morske orgulje ) (below) is an architectural sound art object and an experimental musical instrument, which plays music by way of sea waves and tubes located underneath a set of large marble steps. The waves interact with the organ and create somewhat random but harmonic sounds. It was opened to the public in 2005 following reconstruction work undertaken to repair the devastation Zadar suffered in the Second World War. The Church of St. Donat (below) was built in the early 9th century on the paving stones of the former Roman Forum. It has not been used as a church since 1797 but, because of its good acoustics, concerts are often held there. Outside in the square is a monumental pillar which was used in the Middle Ages as a 'pillar of shame' - remains of chains and hooks which held miscreants in place can still be seen. The Cathedral of St. Anastasia (below) is the largest church in all of Dalmatia (the coastal region of Croatia). The church's origins date back to a Christian basilica built in the 4th and 5th centuries, while much of the currently standing three-nave building was constructed in the Romanesque style during the 12th and 13th centuries. Back in Tisno we tried another fish restaurant which had been recommended to us and met two other guests who were staying at our hotel. They enjoyed food as much as us and we all sat together at one table and had a really fun evening. Far too much wine was imbibed ... We chuckled at the idea of a ' warty venus ' and ordered this dish. When it arrived it contained a selection of seafood - the ' white buzara ' which was made with garlic, olive oil, white wine and parsley and served in a conch (the ' warty venus '). A final view of Tisno harbour before our early morning start the next day back to Split airport. BACK

title: Dublin - 2001
text: Dublin - 2001 Dublin - March 2001 A weekend in Dublin to celebrate the 50th birthday of our friend Marion Hayward with David Granger, David Collins, Gerry Gracias, Stephen Metcalfe, Martin Grocott and Sandra Rainsford plus David's friend ('John from Dublin') and Seán and myself. Our first evening found us in a local bar imbibing the local Liffey water ... After several drinks, things started getting silly ... The next morning, with slightly sore heads, we went out to explore the centre of Dublin - stopping for the obligatory photograph on the footbridge over the River Liffey. Both Stephen and I were immediately attracted to this interesting-looking place. We found a splendidly-named tea shop for Marion - and then I went off to find a bit of 'culture' and found it in Trinity College Library with Ireland’s most prized artifact, the Book of Kells which is an illuminated 680-page version of the four Gospels written in Latin. The 9th century manuscript was composed by monks on vellum and was magnificent to see 'in the flesh'. That evening we went out to dinner which was memorable (sadly for Sandra) as a waitress dropped her tray and a whole plate of pasta went down Sandra's back ... Marion was wearing a feather boa on the second evening and, boys being boys, they all had to try it on. On our final morning, we visited the Oscar Wilde Memorial Sculpture (unveiled in 1997) in Merrion Square, pausing briefly to pose in front of the large fountain in the park.

title: Finland - 1992
text: Finland - 1992 Turku - September 1992 A work trip to Turku in Finland to the wedding celebrations for singer Karita Mattila. My boss, Diana Mulgan, and I jetted off to Turku via Stockholm on 25 September 1992 for a wedding party onboard a ship which took us out to the Finnish Archipelago in the Baltic Sea. Karita was the winner of the inaugural Cardiff Singer-of-the-World competition in 1981 - and Diana was her manager. Even at the competition, Karita had displayed her love of all things pink ... Her wedding outfit also incorporated pink - a pink chicken feather jacket and lots of pearls. Her husband, Tappio, was a used-car salesman who had sold her an upmarket vehicle. It was all rather surreal - the meal basically consisted of herrings (in apple sauce, in mustard, with onions and with a spicy sauce) and potatoes. And lots of vodka. Lots ... In the middle of the Baltic Sea, the ship moored at a small island covered with snow and ice and we all trooped off the boat to dance on the ice - envigorated by the amount of vodka we had consumed. It was about 10 below zero and my camera rather suffered as, after this stop, the mechanism froze and all later photos were superimposed one over the other. Nothing to do with the vodka though ...

title: Galway - 2005
text: Galway - 2005 Galway - April 2005 We (Seán, his sister Marie and I) flew to Shannon to spend a long weekend with friends Geraldine and Niall who live just outside Galway. The first evening we went for a drink at Niall's local golf club. Niall was immediately attracted to my beret which he pinched and then wore for the rest of the evening. The Irish have a seemingly infinite capacity to drink, and we were expected to keep up with them every inch of the way and match them drink for drink ... The next morning found us all with sore heads, but we pressed on and went into Galway city centre to explore. The swans in Galway City are famous. There is a large population of these swans in Galway; they can be fairly friendly, that is if you feed them. After all that excitement it was time to return home for a snooze ... Then a reviving drink (Geraldine makes a mean Cosmopolitan) and then we were whisked off to a German-run, Italian restaurant in the middle of nowhere on The Burren , a bleak area in County Clare. The word 'Burren' comes from an Irish word Boíreann meaning a rocky place. On the way back home in the bus, we were all expected to take a turn at ' the noble call ', ie: in a relatively inebriated state, sing a song, recite a poem and generally entertain the other guests. The next day we drove to the Cliffs of Moher ( Aillte an Mhothair ) which run for about 14 kilometres (9 miles) at the south-western edge of the Burren region in County Clare. The cliffs rank among the most visited tourist sites in Ireland, with around 1.5 million visits per annum and take their name from an old promontory fort called Mothar , now the site of Moher Tower, a ruined Napoleonic-era watchtower. After stopping for a tasty lunch at Moran's Oyster Cottage we returned to Ger and Niall's home.

title: Granada - 2017
text: Granada - 2017 Granada - September 2017 Both Seán and I had been to the Alhambra in the past, but never together. As keen gardeners it was a definite destination for us and we weren't disappointed after our long drive from Mijas. A palace and fortress complex, the Alhambra was originally constructed as a small fortress in 889 AD on the remains of Roman fortifications, and then largely ignored until its ruins were renovated and rebuilt in the mid-13th century by the Nasrid Emir, Mohammed ben Al-Ahmar. It was converted into a royal palace in 1333 by Yusuf I, Sultan of Granada. After the conclusion of the Christian Reconquista in 1492, the site became the Royal Court of Ferdinand and Isabella (where Christopher Columbus received royal endorsement for his expedition), and the palaces were partially altered in the Renaissance style. In 1526 Charles V commissioned a new Renaissance palace better befitting the Holy Roman Emperor in the revolutionary Mannerist style, in direct juxtaposition with the Nasrid Andalusian architecture, but it was ultimately never completed due to Morisco rebellions in Granada which used up all the funds. The Palacio de Carlos V was designed in 1527 by Pedro Machuca (who studied under Michelangelo). The builders ran out of money in 1568 and the palace remained without a roof until the early 20th century when work started again. A fabulous atmospheric place, notable as the major dominant Christian building at the Alhambra. Beyond the Palace is the area which was originally a large soukh or public market square. This faces the Alcazaba (see below), but is now subdivided and obscured by later Christian-era development. The Alhambra resembles many medieval Christian strongholds in its threefold arrangement as a castle, a palace and a residential annex for subordinates. The Alhambra's most westerly feature is the Alcazaba (citadel), a strongly fortified position built on the isolated and precipitous foreland which terminates the plateau on the northwest. There are fabulous views over modern-day Granada to be seen from the citadel. Pretty cooling fountains in the Jardin de los Adarves (Parapet Garden) of the Alcazaba. The Mexuar (or Cuarto Dorado ) is modest in decor and houses the functional areas for conducting business and administration. It was built by Muhammad V, the eldest son and heir of Yusuf I (by his slave Butayna). Born in 1339, he ruled between 1354–1359 and 1362–1391 . The Court of the Myrtles ( Patio de los Arrayanes ) is part of the Palacio de Comares . Its current name is due to the myrtle bushes that surround the central pool, the bright green colour of which contrasts with the white marble of the patio. The pool helped to cool the palace and acted as a symbol of power: because water was usually in short supply, the technology required to keep these pools full was expensive and difficult. The Court of the Lions ( Patio de los Leones ) is an oblong courtyard surrounded by a low gallery supported on 124 white marble columns. In the centre of the court is the Fountain of the Lions , an alabaster basin supported by the figures of twelve lions in white marble - symbols of strength, power and sovereignty. Every hour one lion would produce water from its mouth. The Sala de los Abencerrajes (Hall of the Abencerrages) derives its name from a legend in which the father of Boabdil, the last sultan of Granada, having invited the chiefs of that line to a banquet, massacred them here. This room is a perfect square, with a lofty roof – a dome honeycombed with tiny cells, all different, and said to number 5000 – is an example of the 'stalactite vaulting' of the Moors. The Hamman (Royal Baths) are the only remaining baths of the eight which originally served the 2,000 or so inhabitants of the Alhambra. They were reserved for the sultans’ private use. However, they were an exception since the majority were public and their popularity was linked to pre-prayer body purification rituals. Above we can see the exterior of the roof to the Baths with skylights piercing the roof covering. The private, internalised universe of the Palacio de Los Leones (Palace of the Lions) adjoins the public spaces. These private areas overlook the refined Garden of Lindaraja and the Patio de Daraxa (Court of the Vestibule) . Of the outlying buildings connected to the Alhambra, the foremost in interest is the Palacio de Generalife ("Garden of Arif" or "Garden of the Architect"). The palace and gardens were built during the reign of Muhammed II (1273-1302), Sultan of Granada, and later by Muhammed III (1302–1309). They were redecorated shortly after by Abu I-Walid Isma'il (1313–1324). Much of the garden is a recent reconstruction - commenced in 1931 and completed by Francisco Prieto Moreno in 1951. They are not necessarily 'authentic' - even though they are probably the best known part of the site.

title: Greece 2005
text: Greece - 2005 Greece - October 2005 After a flight and an overnight in Athens with our friends Jenny and Marilyn, we collected our hire car and drove on down to the Peloponnese over the Corinth Canal which connects the Ionian Sea with the Aegean Sea. It cuts through the narrow Isthmus of Corinth and separates the Peloponnese from the Greek mainland, arguably making the peninsula an island. The canal was dug through the isthmus at sea level and has no locks. It is 4 miles long and only 70 foot wide at its base, making it impassable for many modern ships. It has little economic importance and is mainly a tourist attraction. The canal was initially proposed in classical times and a failed effort was made to build it in the 1st century AD. The emperor Nero was the first to attempt to construct the canal, personally breaking the ground with a pickaxe and removing the first basket-load of soil in 67 AD, but the project was abandoned when he died shortly afterwards. Construction recommenced in 1881 but was hampered by geological and financial problems that bankrupted the original builders. It was completed in 1893, but, due to the canal's narrowness, navigational problems, and periodic closures to repair landslides from its steep walls, it failed to attract the level of traffic expected by its operators. We stopped briefly at Ancient Corinth , a city-state of antiquity. The site was occupied from before 3000 BC. In 146 BC, Corinth was captured and was completely destroyed by the Roman army. As a newly rebuilt Roman colony in 44 BC, Corinth flourished and became the administrative capital of the Roman province of Achaea. In 1928, a magnitude 6.3 earthquake devastated the new city, which was then rebuilt on the same site. In 1933, there was a great fire, and the new city was rebuilt again. Driving on down past Kalámata we then arrived at our accommodation at Koróni . The accommodation was fairly basic (terrible plumbing - "no paper down the toilet"!) but it had, as a consolation, some bizarre mushroom lights in the garden. Next morning into the pretty harbour village of Methoni to buy supplies and explore. The Castle of Methoni is a well-preserved medieval fortification which was occupied by the Venetians in c.1700. They added to the ancient battlements and it is still possible to see various Venetian emblems including the winged lion of St. Mark and inscriptions. Then onto Pylos via a wonderful wildlife reserve which included an area of brightly-coloured heathers and other vegetation. The ground underneath was wet and peaty and we had to make our way around it on boardwalks. We then drove into the small town of Pylos and were surprised to see a Russian naval vessel moored up there. It transpired that it was there to celebrate the Battle of Navarino which took place on 20 October 1827, during the Greek War of Independence (1821–32), in Navarino Bay (modern Pylos). Allied forces from Britain, France, and Russia decisively defeated Ottoman and Egyptian forces which were trying to suppress the Greeks. Celebrations are held every year on 20 October (the day we turned up) with delegates from each of the navies. Britain was represented by a submarine which was moored in the Bay.

title: Greece2 2005
text: Greece - 2005 Greece - October 2005 Above Pylos is the Ottoman Neokastro (new castle), which is in a good state of conservation, and looks out onto the island of Sphacteria, the bay of Navarino, and the city. It is one of the best preserved castles in Greece. Inside the walls of the the Ottoman Neokkastro is the well-preserved Church of the Transfiguration of the Saviour , built by the Franks, later transformed into a mosque, then again into a Christian church. A stop on the way back to buy honey from a man selling it at the side of the road. Our next stop was at the town of Nafplio - a pretty place where we had a good meal. The next day we travelled onto Epidaurus to visit the huge theatre. In ancient times, this was said to have delighted Pausanias (a Greek traveler and geographer of the second century AD who lived in the time of Roman emperors Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, and Marcus Aurelius). The ancient theatre of Epidaurus was designed by Polykleitos the Younger in the 4th century BC. The original 34 rows were extended in Roman times by another 21 rows. It seats up to 14,000 people. The theatre is admired for its exceptional acoustics, which permit almost perfect intelligibility of unamplified spoken words from the proscenium to all 14,000 spectators, regardless of their seating. Famously, tour guides have their groups scattered in the stands and show them how they can easily hear the sound of a match struck at centre-stage. Also featuring in the theatre complex was the Stadion (stadium) where running races were held. We then stopped in Gytheio for lunch which was lovely overlooking the harbour. We also found a deserted amphitheatre which was in dire need of restoration. lt was very hot so I took the opportunity to have a swim in the sea. In the second millennium BC, Mycenae was one of the major centres of Greek civilization, a military stronghold which dominated much of southern Greece, Crete, the Cyclades and parts of southwest Anatolia. The first excavations at Mycenae were carried out by Greek archaeologist Kyriakos Pittakis in 1841 where he found and restored the Lion Gate (see below). The main entrance through the circuit wall is made through the best known feature of Mycenae, the Lion Gate , through which passed a stepped ramp leading up to the palace. The Lion Gate was constructed in the form of a 'Relieving Triangle' in order to support the weight of the stones. On the Lion Gate, two lionesses or lions flank the central column, whose significance is much debated. The Mask of Agamemnon is a gold funeral mask discovered at Mycenae by German archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann in 1876. He believed that he had found the body of the King Agamemnon, leader of the Achaeans in Homer's epic of the Trojan War, the Iliad , but modern archaeological research suggests that the mask dates to about 1600 BC, predating the period of the legendary Trojan War by about 400 years. The mask, now displayed in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens, has been described as the "Mona Lisa of prehistory". The Tomb of Clytemnestra (below) The Treasury of Atreus or Tomb of Agamemnon is a large tholos or beehive tomb on Panagitsa Hill, constructed during the Bronze Age around 1250 BC. It was the tallest and widest dome (below) in the world for over a thousand years until construction of the Pantheon in Rome. There is a fascinating museum at the site (although much of the spoils have been taken to the National Archeological Museum in Athens). These human statuettes remain at Mycenae and it is astonishing that some of their skinny arms remain intact.

title: Greece3 2005
text: Greece - 2005 Greece - October 2005 We then arrived back into Athens and visited the Hellenic Parliament where we saw the Evzones, a special unit of the Hellenic Army, also known as Tsoliades , who guard the Monument of the Unknown Soldier in front of the Presidential Mansion. The unusual uniform includes the foustanella , a cotton kilt made from 30 metre s (98 feet) of cloth, with supposedly 400 pleats representing the 400 years of Ottoman occupation and the tsarouchia , red leather clogs with black foundes (pompons). Near the Greek Parliament was a Greek Orthodox church with ornate chandelier and exquisite jewelled icons - and lots of incense . And then onto the Acropolis - Athens' most famous tourist attraction. The Odeon of Herodes Atticus from above. s The Theatre of Dionysus from above. Hadrianic reliefs from the stage front of the Theatre of Dionysus on the South Slope of the Acropolis. The crouching figure in the middle is Silenus "in the attitude of Atlas". The most notable part of the Acropolis is the Parthenon - a former temple dedicated to the goddess Athena, whom the people of Athens considered their patron. Construction began in 447 BC when the Athenian Empire was at the peak of its power. It was completed in 438 BC and is the most important surviving building of Classical Greece, generally considered the zenith of the Doric order. Its decorative sculptures are considered some of the high points of Greek art - but many of which were removed by Lord Elgin and later displayed in the British Museum. Others were removed and are now in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin. The Erechtheion is a temple on the north side of the Acropolis which was dedicated to both Athena and Poseidon. On the north side, there is another large porch with six Ionic columns, and on the south, the famous 'Porch of the Maidens', with six draped female figures (caryatids) as supporting columns. These were notably copied in St. Pancras New Church on the Euston Road in London - built 1819-22 by William and Henry Inwood. There was much restoration work taking place on the Acropolis site with cranes and other heavy lifting equipment reassembling many collapsed structures . Next to the Acropolis site was a fascinating Archeological Museum which was being constructed and extended while we were there. Not all rooms were open at this time. Leaving the Acropolis site, we went down for lunch and had a drink opposite the structure (below). The Choragic Monument of Lysicrates in Plaka, Athens as it is today, and in an engraving from 1840 by W.Richardson. It was erected by Lysicrates, a wealthy patron of musical performances in the Theatre of Dionysus. The monument is known as the first use of the Corinthian order on the exterior of a building. It has been reproduced widely on modern monuments and buildings. The Zappeion is in the National Gardens of Athens. It was built between 1874 and 1888 specifically for the revival of the Olympic Games in the modern world. Unfortunately its benefactor, Evangelis Zappas, did not live long enough to see the Zappeion built. It is now used for meetings and ceremonies. On our final day we drove out to Cape Sounion , east of Athens to see the Temple of Poseidon . A previous visitor to the Temple of Poseidon was Lord Byron who engraved his name on one of the columns supporting the roof. And a final lunch next to the sea before returning to the airport and the flight home ...

title: Ireland - 2017
text: Ireland - 2017 Ireland - July 2017 A ferry crossing from Fishguard to Rosslare for a week's visit to Ireland. To get to Fishguard, we first had to cross the Severn Bridge (the 'new' one) with an attentive pup in the back of the car. We were intrigued by a poster in the window of a shop in Fishguard. Sammy had a rott en crossing (he was sick) but soon recovered and found a cheery welcome from Rose's puppy. Rose is the lady who lets us stay in her apartment in Mijas in Spain. We then visited Garrykennedy on the shores of Lough Derg . In the 15th Century the old Irish clan (the O’Kennedys) built a tower house (below) at the sheltered bay, with which they controlled the strategically important harbour and the surrounding lands. The incursion of Cromwell’s troops put an end to the reign of the clan. Despite the castle's fall the port was always kept in working order. Among other things, slate from nearby mines was shipped across the Shannon to Limerick. I bought two postcards in Garrykennedy which perpetuated the cliché of the Irish living in the 'bog', with ginger hair and going 'fiddly, diddly, dee' all the time ... I t was lovely to stay with Rose in her comfortable house. Sammy liked it too! Putog is a type of Irish black pudding. Rose had some in her fridge so, naturally, we had to take a photo of it. And then onto Oranmore in Galway to stay with Geraldine again. We were lucky when we visited the coast next to Oranmore Castle - to discover it was having an open day. Glorious, unexpected treasures adorn this crazy barn of a castle - now filled with the squeaks of bats, foxes' heads and ferns growing through the stonework. 'Rustic Bohemianism' or certainly 'Shabby Chic' I think they call it ... That evening, Geraldine and Niall held a party to celebrate us coming to stay and to try out their new feature fire wall in the garden. Sammy looked on bemused. One of the other guests was a dancer who had been part of Michael Flatley's 'Riverdance' troupe. After a drink or two, he had his arm twisted to give us a demonstration. Geraldine joined in too ... The next day we drove to Lisdoonvarna ( Lios Dúin Bhearna , meaning "fort of the gapped keep"). The town is famous for its music and festivals. Although the music festival was discontinued in the 1980s, Lisdoonvarna still hosts its annual matchmaking festival in September each year when one of Europe's largest matchmaking events is held in the town attracting upwards of 40,000 romantic hopefuls, bachelor farmers and accompanying revellers. And then to Loop Head where the cliffs at Léim na Leannán (Lovers' Leap) were spectacular. On our way back we stopped at Paddy Burke's in Clarinbridge with its astonishing collection of photos of Noel Coward, Jack Charlton and Samuel Beckett amongs others. Leaving Oranmore and Galway, we then drove down to visit Limerick . A limerick is a type of humorous verse of five lines with an AABBA rhyme scheme: the poem's connection with the city is obscure, but the name is generally taken to be a reference to Limerick city or County Limerick. The earliest known use of the name "Limerick" for this type poem is an 1880 reference, in a Saint John, New Brunswick newspaper, to an apparently well-known tune. Leaving Limerick we then continued on to Thurles in County Tipperary to stay with Veronica Harris, the sister of our Kingsbridge friend Juanita, where we were offered a most hospitable overnight stay. Our final stop was at Kilmuckridge in County Wexford where we had lunch with Geraldine's sister-in-law, Cathy Helly, before heading back to Rosslare to catch the ferry over to Fishguard.

title: Lille - 2001
text: Lille - 2001 Lille - July 2001 We thought we'd try a Eurostar trip to Lille since it seemed such an easy way to get to the city. We were upgraded on the outward journey and received a proper sit-down lunch which was very welcome! Although we arrived into the Eurostar terminal, our hotel was directly opposite Lille-Flandres station which was a very attractive building. The main square in Lille is overlooked by the 104 metre tall Belfry of the Town Hall which gives panoramic views over the local surroundings. The square itself has lots of bars serving the local beer. The Column of the Goddess is the popular name given by the citizens of Lille to the Memorial of the Siege of 1792 which is in the centre of the Grand Place, and has been surrounded by a fountain since 1990. We were surprised to see people doing Argentine Tango in the courtyard of the Town Hall ... The previous time I had been to Lille was to see Rossini's Il Turco in Italia in 1992 at the Lille Opera (below).

title: Portugal - 1992
text: Portugal - 1992 Lisbon - May 1992 A work trip for the premiere of a staged production of Mozart's Cosi fan tutte (conducted by John Eliot Gardiner) at the Teatro Sao Carlos in Lisbon. I managed the singer who was playing Despina. My friend Danny then flew out to meet me as I stayed on for a few days' holiday at the end of the work trip. In 1755 a massive earthquake, and subsequent tidal wave and fire, killed 40,000 people and completely destroyed much of the lower central districts occasioning its rebuilding under the wise instruction of the then prime minister the Marquês de Pombal. Some districts survived the devastation of the earthquake and retain their medieval and sometimes even Moorish structure, notably Alfama . Alfama , the oldest district in Lisbon and crowned with the Castle of St Jorge , is somewhat like a village within a city with labyrinthine streets inaccessible to cars. Great views can be had over the city, including views of the clanky old trams which still run to this day. Construction of the Jerónimos Monastery commenced in 1501 and was completed 100 years later. King Manuel I funded the project with money obtained from the Vintena da Pimenta , a 5 percent tax on commerce from Africa and the Orient, and selected a religious order of Hieronymite monks to occupy the monastery. Their role was to pray for the King's eternal soul and to provide spiritual assistance to navigators and sailors who departed from Lisbon to discover lands around the world. The monastery was designed in a manner that later became known as Manueline : a richly ornate architectural style with complex sculptural themes. We took a train from the central station out to the Torre de Belém . This ornate and distinctively shaped tower was originally designed in 1514 as a formidable fortress and key to the defence of the estuary mouth. The stonework of the exterior is the major attraction with ornate balconies, Manueline (Portuguese late Gothic) rope shapes, animals and shields. Each corner boasts a sentry post with evident Moorish style and from the inside panoramic views of the river and much of the city can be gained.

title: Madrid - 2010
text: Madrid - 2010 Madrid - October 2010 A cultural weekend in Madrid to see the Thyssen-Bornemisza, Prado and Reina Sofia collections and to take in local 'colour' including fan shops and butchery outlets. But the first stop was to a bar for a well-deserved glass of sherry. The Congreso de los Diputados is the lower house of the Spanish parliament and meets in this rather unprepossessing nineteenth century building (plus modern extension - below). The two bronze lions that guard the entrance are made from a melted-down cannon captured during the African War of 1859-60. The Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza is one of the most spectacular collections of private art in the world. Assembled by Baron Heinrich Thyssen-Bornemisza, his son Hans Heinrich and his former beauty-queen wife Carmen, it opened to the public in 1993 and contains pieces by almost every major Western artist since the fourteenth century. Inside I was too astonished by the quality of the artworks on display to remember to take photographs. And then to the Museo del Prado , one of the oldest and greatest collections of art in the world, largely amassed by the Spanish royal family over the last two hundred years. Numerous works by Francisco Goya, the single most extensively represented artist, as well as by Hieronymus Bosch, El Greco, Peter Paul Rubens, Titian, and Diego Velázquez, are some of the highlights of the collection. Photography was forbidden in the Prado but I managed to sneak a crafty (if out of focus) photo of Albrecht Dürer's Portrait of an Unidentified Man of 1521. I particularly wanted to see Dürer's Self Portrait of 1498 which I had admired since I was a schoolboy. The wardens in the room housing this painting were particularly conspicuous so I have to include a photo of this found on the internet. Supper that night was in a local brasserie, noisy but the food (prawns, egg and noodles - not quite sure of the Spanish-ness of this) was delicious. Then a walk back to the hotel via the Plaza Mayor featuring the equestrian statue of King Felipe III which dates from 1616. The next morning included a visit to the Centro de Arte Reina Sofía - an immense exhibition space providing a permanent home for the Spanish collection of modern and contemporary art, inclding the Miró and Picasso legacies. Roy Lichtenstein - Brushstroke (1996) Oskar Schlemmer - Das Triadische Ballett (costume designs) (1922) Superbly displayed and no longer protected by bullet-proof glass and steel girders that once imprisoned it, Picasso's Guernica is a monumental icon of twentieth-century Spanish art and politics which, despite its familiarity, still has the ability to shock. Painted after the bombing of the Basque town of Gernika in April 1937. Joan Miró - Pintura (1925) Benjamín Palencia - Sin título (1935) Man Ray - Object to be Destroyed (1923 - original destroyed 1957) Salvador Dalí - Face of the Great Masturbator (1929) Salvador Dalí - The Enigma of Hitler (1939) Salvador Dalí - Endless Enigma (1938) After all that excitement, it was then time for lunch at a great bar just down the road where they make their own churros in front of customers and which are not fattening at all ...

title: Madrid 2015
text: Madrid - 2015 Madrid - September 2015 My pal Mandy was going to Madrid for a trade fair, so I went with her - neatly avoiding the sales trip - but took her to meet my cousin Jane who lives in Madrid. We met Jane in a bar for breakfast where her husband took her on their first date. She then took us to the Church of San Francisco el Grande , where his family have already booked (and paid for) his funeral mass ... The Church of San Franciso el Grande has been restored over a twenty year period and this magnificent eithteenth-century domed church can now be seen in something close to its original glory. Inside, each of the six chapels is designed in a distinct style ranging from Mozarab and Renaissance to Baroque and Neoclassical. It includes an early Goya painting, The Sermon of San Bernadino of Siena , which itself contains a self-portrait of the 37-year-old artist (in the ochre suit on the extreme right). By then we were hungry again and stopped at a fabulous indoor market where food stalls sold a variety of delicious treats to tempt us - which naturally we had to try. Crossing the Plaza Mayor , we found a superb hat shop and a bizarre woman dressed as a giant rabbit covered with blue tinsel. Even my cousin who lived in Madrid didn't understand what this was about ... Part museum and part art gallery, the Museo Sorolla is a tribute to an artist's life and work and is one of Madrid's most underrated treasures. Situated in Joaquin Sorolla's former home, it is a delightful oasis of peace and tranquility with a shady Andalusian-style courtyard, an art gallery of his work and extensive collection of trinkets from around the world.

title: Madrid 2015B
text: Madrid - 2015 Madrid - September 2015 On Sunday, while my pal was at her trade fair, I took a train from Madrid up to El Escorial , the historical residence of the King of Spain, in the town of San Lorenzo de El Escorial, about 28 miles north-west of Madrid. It also functions as a monastery, basilica, royal palace, pantheon, library, museum, university, school and hospital. Philip II of Spain (who reigned 1556–1598) engaged the Spanish architect Juan Bautista de Toledo to be his collaborator in the building of the complex at El Escorial. Toledo had spent the greater part of his career in Rome, where he had worked on St. Peter's Basilica, and in Naples, where he had served the king's viceroy, whose recommendation brought him to the king's attention. Philip appointed him architect-royal in 1559, and together they designed El Escorial as a monument to Spain's role as a centre of the Christian world. However, Toledo did not live to see the completion of the project. With his death in 1567, direction passed to his apprentice, Juan de Herrera, under whom the building was completed in 1584, in just under 21 years. To this day, la obra de El Escorial ("the work of El Escorial") is a proverbial expression for a thing that takes a long time to finish. The floor plan of the building is in the form of a grid-iron. The traditional belief is that this design was chosen in honour of St. Lawrence, who, in the third century AD, was martyred by being roasted to death on a grill. St. Lawrence’s feast day is 10 August, the same date as the 1557 Battle of St. Quentin. However, a more persuasive theory for the origin of the floor plan is that it is based on descriptions of the Temple of Solomon by the Judeo-Roman historian, Flavius Josephus: a portico followed by a courtyard open to the sky, followed by a second portico and a second courtyard leading to the "holy of holies". Statues of David and Solomon on either side of the entrance to the basilica of El Escorial lend further weight to the theory that this is the true origin of the design. El Escorial has been the burial site for most of the Spanish kings of the last five centuries, Bourbons as well as Habsburgs. The Royal Pantheon contains the tombs of the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V (who ruled Spain as King Charles I), Philip II, Philip III, Philip IV, Charles II, Louis I, Charles III, Charles IV, Ferdinand VII, Isabella II, Alfonso XII, and Alfonso XIII. However, two Bourbon kings, Philip V (who reigned from 1700 to 1724) and Ferdinand VI (1746–1759), as well as King Amadeus (1870–1873), are not buried in the monastery. The coffins are already constructed which means future monarchs who die have to fit into those pre-made coffins. So, when a monarch dies, they are put in a special 'rotting chamber' called a pudridero , and they are left there for about 40 years until they are just bones. Then the bones are placed inside the coffin. The parents of the current King (Juan Carlos I) are currently both in the rotting chamber, and will take the final two slots available in the special burial room (26 total). This means the Juan Carlos has to pick another place to be buried, since El Escorial is now 'out of space'. Christ Crowned with Thorns is an oil on panel painting made in the 1530s by a follower of Hieronymus Bosch. The main scene is set in a circular tondo with a gold background. The man in the green on the left at the back is a dead-ringer for Jim Broadbent. It is an elaborated version of another Bosch's composition of the same subject held in the National Gallery, London, combining two events from Biblical account of the Passion of Jesus: the Mocking of Jesus and the Crowning with Thorns. That evenings after our respective businesses of the day, we went out for supper and enjoyed some "typical Galician octopus" and chorizo - passing a fabulous wine room in the restaurant (below). We had a chorizo starter (it just came as a giant slab of sausage) and the octopus "a feira - sliced at the moment". Again, it was huge - but delicious - and needed lashings of rioja to wash it down. The next morning, our heads suffering a little, we did a quick flit round the Reina Sofia collection before retiring for brunch at the same cafe I had been to five years previously and, once again, sampled their selection of churros.

title: Majorca - 2001
text: Majorca - 2001 Majorca - June 2001 A group of six of us rented a villa in Pollença in Majorca and flew out to Palma where we collected a hire car. On our first afternoon we went into the local town to buy provisions (ie: crisps, wine and chocolate) and do a bit of exploring. The villa was large and fairly comfortable and had a super pool area of which we made good use. Some behaved more like children than others ... One day, Seán and I went off to explore the island on our own. Sitting on the top of a mountain overlooking the surrounding countryside off the road between Porto Colom and Felanitx, we discovered the Monastery of San Salvador . The views from the Monastery were truly stunning, and they also had a very welcome café where we enjoyed lunch with the best view of the holiday. We continued driving after our lunch and came to the Caves of Drach ( Coves del Drac - lit. 'Dragon caves') which are four great caves which extend to a depth of 25 m and are approximately 4 km in length. Pressing onwards, we came to the Santuari de Lluc - another monastery / sanctuary which was founded in the 13th century after a Moorish shepherd found a statue of the Virgin Mary on this site. Lluc is considered to be the most important pilgrimage site on Majorca. It is also known for its boys' choir, Els Blauets (a name derived from the blue cassocks worn by the boys), which was founded in 1531. And, finally, we made it to Palma Cathedral - but the vergers were clearing the building as we arrived so we only had a couple of minutes to look around inside and therefore our photos are mostly of the exterior. Another visit clearly beckons ... Back at the villa, we enjoyed the beautiful bougainvillea which was growing around the gateway to the garden.

title: Mijas
text: Mijas Mijas - September 2013 Our friend, Rose from Nenagh in Ireland, was kind enough to let us stay in her lovely apartment on the edge of a golfcourse at Mijas (near Málaga) in Spain. It had a fabulous pool and great views over the local mountains. In the mountain village of Mijas, we found what became a favourite restaurant of ours and to which we have returned on each subsequent trip. The food is simple but always delicious. September is Seán's birthday month, and Rose and one of Sean's best friends (Geraldine) surprised him by flying out to the apartment to see him. We went into Fuengirola for drinks and a slap-up supper. A quick word with the waiter and a surprise birthday cake appeared ... The next day we went to the beach - another place to which we return every time we go to Rose's apartment. It has a super beach bar where we can get lunch and cold beers to keep us cool. After a hard day at the beach, it was time for another trip into Fuengirola for drinks at the local Irish bar - where else? The next day Rose and Geraldine had to fly back to Ireland. We returned to the beach after seeing them off safely. On our final evening there was a magnificent sunset. Mijas - September 2015 It was a delight to return to the apartment two years later where we found it as lovely as before. Up to Mijas to our favourite restaurant again. These (below) were lightly fried zuccini with a honey and balsamic glaze. Then a seafood paella and grilled hake. A truck which made us laugh as 'Bimbo' clearly means something different in Spanish ... One day we drove into Málaga to visit the Cathedral which was constructed between 1528 and 1782, following the Renaissance-style plans drawn by Diego de Siloe. The north tower is 84 metres (276 ft) high, making this building the second-highest cathedral in Andalusia, after the Giralda of Seville. The south tower remains unfinished. To defray the enormous expenses of the work the Crown, after the War of Succession, imposed an excise duty or tax on all ships that called in Málaga. The rather mawkish Beheading of Saint Paul was painted by Enrique Simonet in 1887. Málaga is home to the Picasso Museum which holds some fantastic works of his. Paul on a Donkey (1923) and Olga, Portrait of a Woman (1923) Portrait of Dora Maar (1943) and Seated Figure (1971) When we visited, the Picasso Museum was holding an exhibition of sculptures by French-born American sculptor Louise Bourgeois which I had seen when it had been shown at Tate Modern in London. The hot sunny climate in Málaga gave them a completely different emphasis. Above are Spider (1994-1999) and The Couple (2003). Another day, another beach! Another year, another birthday! Near Rose's apartment is an outlet which sells ornaments and columns for gardens and installations. These fingers take us by surprise every time we see them! But who on earth would put them in their garden? We found some party hats in a cupboard so decided to "party in pink" ! Mijas - September 2017 Another two years whizzed by before we were able to return to 'Las Golondrinas'. A wide variety of holiday reading for the week, while Seán makes a delicious tortilla for lunch. Up to Mijas to our favourite restaurant again (we both had the same this time) and then a walk around the village found some locals who had come in on horseback. A bank window sums up Andalusia perfectly: religion, charcuterie and salsa lessons ! This year we drove into Marbella on a Sunday and found it fairly deserted but very hot. These street sculptures (above) were by Salvador Dalí. A nice place for ice cream in the shade while we listened to a service through the open doors of the local church, the Iglesia Mayor de la Encarnacion . It was a great shame that the local macramé shop was closed on a Sunday, otherwise we might have bought up all the stock ...! Delicious meals eaten on the terrace and, bottom right, at the local roadside café. A final day lazing on our favourite beach . The 'finger store' was still selling their digits - we wondered if you had to buy them in sets of five! Our last evening with warm breezes and a beautiful sunset .

title: Nuremberg - 1996
text: Nuremberg - 1996 Nuremberg - February 1996 I had gone to Munich for a weekend of opera - Il barbiere di Siviglia on the Friday and Handel's Serse on the following Monday. With a free day on Saturday, I took the train to Nuremberg to visit the birthplace and home of my idol, Albrecht Dürer (1471–1528). Dürer was Germany's most famous artist, and he lived and worked in this massive half-timbered house for nearly 20 years, from 1509 onwards. This is one of the few surviving burgher houses from Nuremberg’s golden age and, even more significantly, is the only surviving 15th century artist's house in Northern Europe. Johann Heinrich Hintze - Albrecht Dürer's House on Thiergärtnertorplatz (around 1830). The Imperial City of Nuremberg tried in 1627 to persuade Bavarian Elector Maximilian I not to take away Dürer's famous Four Apostles of 1526 for his Munich collection, offering superbly crafted copies instead. That effort failed. But the city then conceived a desire to keep Dürer’s paintings in some form, if only in acceptable copies. Thus over the centuries a substantial collection has developed that uniquely conveys a cross-section of Dürer’s oeuvre of paintings. However, Nuremberg is also known for other, less uplifting, reasons: the most notorious being the location of the Nazi Party Rally Grounds (German: Reichsparteitagsgelände , literally: Reich Party Congress Grounds) which covered about 11 square kilometres to the southeast of Nuremberg. Six Nazi party rallies were held there between 1933 and 1938. I took a train out to the Rally Grounds to see for myself. The entire 7-square-mile site was designed by chief Nazi architect Albert Speer with close input from Adolf Hitler. The site was designed on a grand scale to dwarf the size of the individual participants and to herd them into larger groups to foster collective solidarity and included many elements of Nazi architecture: a neoclassical style with a strong, utilitarian function.

title: Palermo - 1982
text: Palermo - 1982 Palermo - May 1982 A trip to Palermo to visit college friends James Schofield and Janette Ringsell who were then teaching English in Sicily - flying out from Luton with Janette's mother Cathy. We arrived on the day after the murder of Pio La Torre (Communist 'mayor' of Palermo) by the Mafia - hence the protests and red flags in the main square. While in Palermo I was able to attend a performance of Bellini's I Capuleti e I Montecchi at the Teatro Massimo - a resplendent opera house built between 1874-1897. Dedicated to King Victor Emanuel II, it is the largest opera house in Italy and renowned for its perfect acoustics. Santa Rosalia is the patron saint of Palermo as, in 1624 when a plague beset Palermo, she appeared to a hunter, to whom she indicated where her remains were to be found. She ordered him to bring her bones to Palermo. The hunter climbed the mountain and found her bones in the cave as described. After her remains were carried around the city three times, the plague ceased. After this Saint Rosalia was venerated as the patron saint of Palermo and a sanctuary was built in the cave where her remains were discovered. In 1825, geologist William Buckland was in Palermo on holiday and asked to see the bones of the saint. After examinating the relics the geologist determined them to be "non-human", in fact he declared the relics were actually the bones of a goat. According to Buckland, priests said that the saint would not let him see her remains because he was not a Catholic Christian, and locked the relics away from people's eyes. The Capuchin Catacombs of Palermo ( Catacombe dei Cappuccini ) are burial catacombs which provide a somewhat macabre tourist attraction. The monastery outgrew its original cemetery in the 16th century and monks began to excavate crypts below it. In 1599 they mummified one of their number, recently dead brother Silvestro of Gubbio who was the first occupant. Bodies were dehydrated on the racks of ceramic pipes in the catacombs and sometimes later washed with vinegar. Some of the bodies were embalmed and others enclosed in sealed glass cabinets. Originally the catacombs were intended only for the dead friars. However, in the following centuries it became a status symbol to be entombed into the Capuchin catacombs. One day we made an excursion to Segesta - an archaeological site which features an unusually well-preserved Doric temple, thought to have been built in the 420 BC by an Athenian architect, and a Greek theatre. The temple lacks any ornamentation, altar or deity dedication, and was never roofed over. It did however escape destruction by the Carthaginians in the late 5th century. On our way back to Palermo, we stopped at the small fishing village of Mondello in the shadow of Mount Gallo where I took the opportunity to have a dip. The Italians were shocked as they never go in the sea before the beginning of June as it was "too cold until then". To me, however, it was perfect. According to a legend, William II of Sicily fell asleep under a carob tree while hunting in the woods near Monreale. The Holy Virgin appeared to him in dream, suggesting he built a church there. The legend continues that, after removing the tree, a treasure was found in its roots, whose golden coins were used to finance the construction. The resulting Duomo di Monreale , begun in 1174, is considered one of the greatest existent examples of Norman architecture. The apartment in which James and Janette lived was very noisy: it was directly over a road crossing and all Italian drivers seemed to think sounding their car horn was more important than slowing down at the junction. On our final evening we bought pizza to eat in the kitchen. One piece was dropped on the floor and we obviously thought nothing of washing it off and hanging it out on the washing line to dry ...

title: Paris 1979
text: Paris - 1979 Paris - May 1979 My first visit to Paris. Having been to see Kate Bush perform at the London Palladium and blagging our way into a back-stage party, we met her and were invited to come to see her perform at the Theatre des Champs-Élysées. My old school friend Jonathan and I went over to France with Louise, whom we had met at the Palladium concerts. The view from Notre-Dame Cathedral was impressive - the Pompidou Centre one way (above) and the Église Saint-Sulpice the other (below). Across the River Seine was the Eiffel Tower which we visited after our trip up Notre-Dame. The concert was great fun, especially as we went with Jonathan's French aunt, Vita, who got us in via the back-stage door by pretending she was the 'Minister of Culture' ... Not a woman to be trifled with!

title: Paris 1979B
text: Paris - 1979 Paris - August 1979 In August, I returned to Paris when a group of us drove a mini-bus to Italy. Our first stop of this 'epic trip' was Paris. I found a furniture store which had a chair which was just crying out for someone to sit on it ... Then Pepin and I pretended to be classical sculptures on the benches outside N otre-Dame Cathedral . It seemed funny at the time. Less so now. The major reason for our stop in Paris was to visit the Paris / Moscow 1900-1930 exhibition at the Pompidou Centre . Also on the trip was my room-mate, Guy who was an architecture student (hence his effortless style), Pepin and Penny (co-students on my History of Art course) and Tom who was then going out with Pepin's sister, Emma.

title: Paris 1981
text: Paris - 2004 Paris - April 1981 A visit to Paris with my friend Jackie, to see the ballet L'Arlesienne at the Chatelet Theatre (and a tour of the Paris Opéra where we saw Ruggero Raimondi in rehearsal). Lots of odd Parisian window dressing and the obligatory visit to the Pompidou Centre where, as a non-smoker, I posed in front of Claes Oldenburg's Colossal Ashtray . Plus visits to the Eiffel Tower, Place Vendôme and the Champs-Élysées. 'Best Kitch' inde ed ...

title: Paris 2004
text: Paris - 2004 Paris - August 2004 A long weekend visit to see friends of Faye (Seán's niece) and her husband Paul, who were living in Paris - and to do a bit of exploring ourselves. The River Seine is attractive at any time of the year and the Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Paris is considered to be one of the finest examples of French Gothic architecture. Several of Faye's friends were going to a party - although quite why they were dressed as milk-maids (from Brittany or Normandy?) escapes me. We found an excellent restaurant for our first evening's meal . Next day we visited the Sacré-Cœur Basilica which is dedicated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus. It is located at the summit of Montmartre, the highest point in the city. If you look closedly (above) you can see Seán in yellow posing on the steps to the Basilica. At the base of the Eiffel Tower - named after the engineer Gustave Eiffel, whose company designed and built the tower between 1887 and 1889. We then walked to the Parc André Citroën , a 14 hectare park located on the left bank of the river Seine. It was built on the site of a former Citroën automobile manufacturing plant, the park is named after company founder André Citroën. A brief glimpse of the Musée du Louvre (allegedly the world's largest art museum) and the then newly-installed Louvre Pyramid , a large glass and metal pyramid designed by architect I. M. Pei. The large pyramid serves as the main entrance to the museum. Then to the Jardin des Tuileries (below) which is located between the Louvre and the Place de la Concorde. Created by Catherine de' Medici as the garden of the Tuileries Palace in 1564, it was eventually opened to the public in 1667 and became a public park after the French Revolution.

title: Paris

title: Prague - 2004
text: Prague - 2004 Prague - December 2004 I had previously been to Prague in 1991 for a performance of Don Giovanni at the Estates Theatre (where it received its premiere back in 1787). This time, Seán and I went for a pre-Christmas break. We were impressed with Prague's tram system which took us into Staromák (the Old Town Square), the historic square in the Old Town quarter. We saw the Prague Orloj , a medieval astronomical clock mounted on the Old Town Hall and then walked to Charles Bridge, a medieval stone arch bridge that crosses the Vltava (Moldau) river. Its construction started in 1357 under the auspices of King Charles IV, and finished in the early 15th century. On our way to Prague Castle we saw these buskers. The Castle is the official office of the President of the Czech Republic and was previously a seat of power for kings of Bohemia, Holy Roman emperors and presidents of Czechoslovakia. The Bohemian Crown Jewels are kept within a hidden room inside it. According to the Guinness Book of Records , Prague Castle is the largest ancient castle in the world. Within the walls of Prague Castle is the Cathedral of Saint Vitus . which is a prominent example of Gothic architecture and is the largest and most important church in the country. Containing the tombs of many Bohemian kings and Holy Roman Emperors, the cathedral is under the ownership of the Czech government as part of the Prague Castle complex. Czech TV was broadcasting a concert from the Cathedral which these crazy tourists thought worth photographing, while Seán looked on from the background. The Municipal House ( Obecní dum ) is a civic building housing Smetana Hall, which serves as a concert hall and ballroom. The Royal Court palace used to be located on the same site and from 1383 until 1485 the King of Bohemia lived in the property. It was demolished in the early 20th century and construction of the current building started in 1905 and houses artwork by Alfons Mucha, Jan Preisler and Max Švabinský although we were unable to see these. We did however get to visit the fabulous café with its resplendant art deco light fittings. As well as its famous tram system, Prague has a Metro. This particular station had a very Soviet-looking style - or perhaps a stage set from Doctor Who ...

title: Italy - 1995
text: Italy - 1995 Rome and Florence - January 1995 While it wasn't exactly snowing when we came to Rome, it was about as cold as I had ever been. I'd come with my colleague, Shirley, for a performance of Berlioz's opera Benvenuto Cellini at the Rome Opera. Scrambling around to try and see as much of the ancient city centre in a very short period, we found the church of San Pietro in Vincoli (Saint Peter in Chains), best known for being the home of Michelangelo's statue of Moses , part of the tomb of Pope Julius II. A quick flit to the Trevi Fountain in the bright winter sunshine. We WERE there - even only if in silhouette! And then onto Florence for an afternoon concert of La damnation de Faust (also by Berlioz), so we were able to see the sights (Ponte Vecchio etc) before the performance. The Duomo (above left), the Palazzo Vecchio (above right) and the Church of Santa Maria Novella (below). There is a life-size statue of the sculptor and jeweller Benvenuto Cellini in a niche outside the Uffizi Galleries. After the afternoon concert, Shirley and I were free to go out to dinner. We walked back to the hotel after this and had a bit of fun along the way with Il Porcellino ("piglet") a bronze copy of a cast by Pietro Tacca (1577–1640) made about 1634. Tacca's bronze was originally intended for the Boboli Gardens. Visitors to Il Porcellino put a coin into the boar's gaping jaws, with the intent to let it fall through the underlying grating for good luck, and they rub the boar's snout to ensure a return to Florence, a tradition that the Scottish literary traveller Tobias Smollett noted in 1766, which has kept the snout in a state of polished sheen while the rest of the boar's body has patinated to a dull brownish-green ...

title: Rome
