title: Ronda - 2013
text: Ronda - 2013 Rond a - September 2013 The previous time I had been to Ronda was back in February 1985 (28 years earlier!) when the bus ride up from Marbella was alarming, veering over precipitous drops over the cliff-side road. Metal barriers had since been installed along the side of the road, so it now felt a little bit safer. Ronda itself didn't seem to have changed much. The Puente Nuevo (New Bridge) still spans the canyon although the term 'nuevo' is something of a misnomer, as the building of this bridge commenced in 1751 and took until 1793 to complete. It towers 120 metres (390 feet) above the canyon floor. The former town hall, which stands next to the Puente Nuevo, is now the site of a parador and has a view of the Tajo canyon. We had lunch at an ideally-situated restuarant with fabulous views but with, sadly, a nearby wasps' nest so we had to retreat inside the building to avoid being stung during our lunch. Shops sold all sorts of items - flamenco dresses (all toning - naturally) and delicatessens with huge ranges of jamon, cheese, wine and bottled goods. We were perplexed by this sign as a collection of 'sludge' did not sound particularly enticing. This turned out to be a poor translation as the The Museum of Popular Arts and Customs had a collection of clay figures that are known as the Barros Malagueños . This artform had its origin in Naples, and began to become popular in Málaga at the end of the 18th century. The first figures were made on religious themes, but following Goya's populism, interest turned to creating scenes of daily life and local and national folklore. Ronda has many cultural associations: Ernest Hemingway's novel For Whom the Bell Tolls describes the execution of Nationalist sympathizers early in the Spanish Civil War. The Republicans murder the Nationalists by throwing them from cliffs in an Andalusian village, and Hemingway allegedly based the account on killings that took place in Ronda at the cliffs of El Tajo. Orson Welles was said to be inspired by his frequent trips to Spain and Ronda (including his unfinished film Don Quixote ). After he died in 1985, his ashes were buried in a well on the rural property of his friend, retired bullfighter Antonio Ordoñez. In a charming orange-tree lined square we found the Iglesia de Santa Maria la Mayor . The city’s original mosque metamorphosed into this elegant church. Just inside the entrance is an arch covered with Arabic inscriptions that was part of the mosque’s mihrab (prayer niche indicating the direction of Mecca). The interior is a riot of decorative styles and ornamentation and a huge central cedar choir stall divides the church into two sections: aristocrats to the front, everyone else at the back . We then visited the Iglesia del Esp’ritu Santo , which is unique in being part of the original fortified walls of the old city. The church was built on the destroyed foundations of an octagonal tower used by the moors to defend the gate and walls in this part of Ronda. King Ferdinand ordered its construction after seizing Ronda and it took 20 years to complete and was consecrated on Whitsunday 1505. It was possible to visit the bell tower (the small window top middle of photo, below) but the bell was rung automatically by a system powered by electricity. It did give, however, excellent views over the surrounding countryside.

title: Rovinj 2009
text: Rovinj - 2009 Rovinj - July 2009 The previous year, in 2008 when we had gone to Egypt, we had flown down over the coast of Croatia and remarked on how beautiful it looked. 2009 found us in Croatia itself to find out first-hand. Our destination was Rovinj (pronounced Ro-VEEN). In Italy, of which it used to be part, it is called Rovigno. We had booked a second floor apartment overlooking the harbour - with a roof terrace which gave us terrific views and was a beautiful place to sit with a glass of wine in the evening. After unpacking, we immediately went down into the harbour area to explore and took a passenger ferry out to one of the local islands ( Sveti Andrija ) for a swim. One day, after our swim, we returned to find filming taking place by the local TV company with photogenic presenters and featuring local customs, foods, 'peasant dancing' and gymnastics. Rovinj was endlessly interesting as there were so many hidden aspects to be seen at different times of the day, giving a variety of views under differing light conditions. The Church of Saint Euphemia can be seen from virtually every aspect in Rovinj and her statue on the campanile acts as a weather vane as she changes direction depending on the wind. Euphemia was martyed by the Governor of Chalcedon (near Istanbul in Turkey) in AD 304, having been discovered with forty-nine other Christians hiding in a house and worshipping God. She was placed in the arena, where lions were released to kill her, but instead they licked her wounds. It is believed that she finally died of wounds from a wild bear. Christians from Chalcedon preserved her body until AD 620 when the town was captured by the Persians. The sarcophagus with the body of St. Euphemia was then transferred to Constantinople. In AD 800 the Iconoclasts came to power, and the Christians were forced to remove her relics. Legend is that her marble sarcophagus came floating in the sea to the coast of Rovinj after a storm. Many people tried to haul the sarcophagus to the Church of Saint George, but no one succeded. Finally, answering St. Euphemia's call, a small boy with two cows managed to haul the sarcophagus up the hill. The people of Rovinj considered it a miracle, and proclaimed St. Euphemia the patron-saint of the town. Her day is celebrated on September 16. Traditionally, on St. Euphemia's Day people eat mutton with sauerkraut ( ovca z kapuzom ) and fritule an Istrian delicacy. We also took a boat up to Trieste which is only 30km to the north - but is in fact in Italy. The boat stopped at a third country - Slovenia - on the way. Trieste was one of the oldest parts of the Habsburg Monarchy, belonging to it from 1382 until 1918. In the 19th century Trieste became the fourth largest city of the Austro-Hungarian Empire (after Vienna, Budapest and Prague). In the fin de siècle period at the end of the 19th century it emerged as an important hub for literature and music. The 'Monument to the Fallen Soldiers in the First World War' is in the Parco della Rimembranza. The sculpture was inaugurated before King Victor Emmanuel III and numerous high-ranking fascist officials in 1935. Preparations were underway for a festival of some kind, but we never did find out exactly what. After lots of exploring (including seeing the statue of James Joyce - above), we were ready to sit down and enjoy a drink. NEXT

title: Rovinj2 2009
text: Rovinj - 2009 Rovinj - July 2009 Julian and I went off on the bus one day to Porec to visit the Euphrasian Basilica - built and dedicated to Mary in the sixth century during the period of Bishop Euphrasius. It was built from 553 on the site of the older basilica that had become dilapidated. For the construction, parts of the former church were used and the marble blocks were imported from the coast of the Sea of Marmara. The wall mosaics were executed by Byzantian masters. The construction took about ten years. Inside, the two aisles are separated from the nave by 18 elegant Greek marble colonnades with richly sculpted Byzantine and Romanesque capitals, decorated with depictions of animals. They all carry the monogram of Saint Euphrasius. The arches between the capitals are decorated with stucco work. The most striking feature of the basilica are its mosaics which date from the 6th century, and which are thought to be by the same craftsmen who created the mosaics at Ravenna. The mosaics in the triumphal arch over the apse represent Christ; holding an opened book with the Latin text "Ego sum lux vera" ("I am the true light") with the Apostles, each with their attribute. The apse is dominated by the marble ciborium , modelled after the one in St. Mark's in Venice, it was built in 1277 on the orders of Otto, Bishop of Porec. The canopy, decorated with mosaics, is carried by four marble columns that belonged to the previous 6th-century ciborium. We hired a car one day, and set off into the Croatian 'hinterland'. Our first stop was at Buje , known as the "sentinel of Istria" for its hilltop site, and home to the Church of Mater Misericordiae (The Mother of Sorrows). Then onto Groznjan , known as the "town of artists" which has about 20 art galleries, hosts a summer film school and has become an international centre of Croatian music. Groznjan also has an annual jazz festival attracting international musicians, such as Georgie Fame in 2007. Then to Hum where we climbed an extremely steep hill but found a wonderful restaurant for lunch with a spectacular view. And, finally, to Buzet before returning back to Rovinj. Our final jaunt was a day trip to Pula where we visited the Roman Amphitheatre. On our way we stopped off in the town of Vodnjan where we saw the very Venetian-looking Town Hall in People's Square (below). Many old native residents speak an Istriot language they call Bumbaro. These inhabitants are called the Bumbari. The Church of St. Biagio (Saint Blaise), the biggest church in Istria is built on remnants of an early Romanesque church that was torn down in 1781. It also houses a sacred art collection which specialises in numerous relics and the mummified bodies of saints, reliquaries from Murano, habits of the saints and valuable old books. We paid our money, were taken behind a screen and then the curator lifted a curtain to show a macabre display of skeletons and mummified saintly bodies. And then to Pula itself. We chuckled at the names on a door buzzer next to where we parked the car, before we walked into the centre where we saw the Temple of Augustus which was dedicated to the first Roman emperor, Augustus, and probably built during the emperor's lifetime at some point between 27 BC and his death in AD 14. The Arch of the Sergii is an Ancient Roman triumphal arch which commemorates three members of the Sergii family, specifically Lucius Sergius Lepidus, a tribune serving in the twenty-ninth legion that participated in the Battle of Actium and disbanded in 27 BC. This suggests an approximate date of construction: 29–27 BC. The arch stood behind the original naval gate of the early Roman colony. The Sergii were a powerful family of officials in the colony and retained their power for centuries. The Pula Arena is a Roman amphitheatre which is the only remaining Roman amphitheatre to have four side towers entirely preserved. It was constructed between 27 BC and AD 68, and is among the world's six largest surviving Roman arenas. When we visited, the arena was being used for a music and film festival (Elton John had performed live on 8 July 2009) so the centre was full of temporary seating. The arena has also been used for cinematic works such as Titus , a 1999 film adaptation of Shakespeare's tragedy Titus Andronicus by Julie Taymor. Astonishingly, two professional ice hockey games were also played there in September 2012. As with many Roman buildings, it provided work for out-of-work actors to dress up and pretend to be Roman centurions or serving maids etc. The arena is open to the public daily, and the underground passages below the arena house exhibitions of viticulture and olive growing in Istria. BACK

title: Sardinia - 2008
text: Sardinia - 2008 Sardinia - August 2008 After a flight to Cagliari and then a wild taxi ride to Calasetta on the small island of Sant'Antioco off the south-west coast of Sardinia which we crossed by a causeway, our first evening found us enjoying a Serata Gastronomica in the gloriously-namd Piazza Belly. We enjoyed cassulli al sugo di pecora (pasta with lamb sauce) and a glass of wine and lightly-fried doughnuts to follow. The next morning was hot and sunny and we made our way down to the local beach - Spiaggia Sottotorre - which had crystal clear water and lovely soft sand (and a convenient café for coffee and cake). We walked back into town and saw lots of the local flora including Sardinian Myrtle ( Myrtus comunis ), the berries of which are used to make a liqueur. The Savoy Tower of Calasetta was an easily recognisable landmark. Built in 1729 as a watchtower against attacks from the sea, mainly at the hands of Arab pirates, it is constructed of red trachyte and stands at the highest point of the town and overlooks the beautiful beach of Sottotorre. Back to the apartment to enjoy evening views over Calasetta from the balcony. One day we took the ferry over to Isola di San Pietro to the tiny port of Carloforte. But first we had to stop for a coffee and to watch the world go by. From Carloforte we took another boat for a trip around the island . It was baking hot on board and the boat stopped at one point to allow us all to dive into the sea to cool off. Back then onto the ferry which took us on the return journey to Calasetta. This time there seemed to be a lot of nuns on board ... Ian is notoriously shy at being photographed. Here he is in the apartment but, after a glass or two of the local vino, I persuaded him to emerge from behind his cushions. My final morning and there seemed to be a fire somewhere in the distance. I never did find out what caused this.

title: Scandinavia - 1997
text: Scandinavia - 1997 Stockholm and Copenhagen - February 1997 A work trip to Stockholm for meetings with the Drottningholm Opera and Svenska Rikskonserter. Bizarrely, I stayed in a hotel which had been converted from a prison ... Stockholm city centre was smart and very business-orientated - but very cold! After my meetings I took a 35 minute flight over to Copenhagen where I met with my pal Ian, who was there for his own work meetings the following day. While he was doing those, I explored Copenhagen town centre which seemed similar in many respects to Stockholm . The Tivoli Gardens are a world-famous amusement park and pleasure garden. The park opened on 15 August 1843 and is the third-oldest operating amusement park in the world, after Dyrehavsbakken in nearby Klampenborg, also in Denmark, and Wurstelprater in Vienna. We met for lunch and then saw this marvellous spectacle: children beating the hell out of a container filled with oranges until it broke and all the fruit cascaded out. Similar to the piñata tradition from Mexico, the Danish version is called slå katten af tønden ("hit the cat out of the barrel") in which a wooden barrel is struck to release candy or, in this case, fruit . Our final night in Copenhagen was spent at Det Kongelige Teater (Old Stage) to see Poulenc's Dialogues of the Carmelites .

title: Seville - 2013
text: Seville - 2013 Seville - September 2013 We drove up from Mijas to Seville, leaving the car in an enormous underground carpark. We visited the Bullring ( Plaza de toros de la Real Maestranza de Caballería de Sevilla ) - a 12,000-capacity circular ring on which construction began in 1749 to replace the rectangular bullring that was previously located there. We thought its baroque facade looked like a surprised owl. The inner facade of the plaza (called the Palco del Príncipe or Prince's Box) was completed in 1765. This 'box' consists of two parts: the access gate through which the successful bull-fighters exit, and the theatre box itself, which is reserved for the exclusive use of the Spanish Royal Family. The Palco was built for the Infante de España, Felipe de Borbón, son of Felipe V and Isabel de Farnesio. Below ground level there was another world - stables for the horses, enclosures for the bulls and an exhibition which included paintings of famous bulls, costumes worn by celebrated toreadors and a chapel where bull-fighters prayed for success and that they would not be gored by the bull. Time for lunch and we were pleased to stumble across this charming little bar which did an excellent meal for us - with a glass of ice-cold white Rioja. The Metropol Parasol , 6 giant wooden mushrooms – popularly known as Las Setas de la Encarnación (The Mushrooms of the Incarnation), form one of the newest architectural structures in Seville, serving as a shelter from the heat during the day and gathering families in the afternoon and evening. It’s a fabulous wooden structure, although it looks metallic and was designed by the German architect Jürgen Mayer and completed in April 2011 and claims to be the largest wooden structure in the world. Its appearance, location, delays and cost overruns in construction resulted in much public controversy. After its completion in the early 16th century, Seville Cathedral ( Catedral de Santa María de la Sede ), supplanted Istanbul's Hagia Sophia as the largest cathedral in the world. It was built on the site of the earlier Almohad mosque. Seville Cathedral was the site of the baptism of Infant Juan of Aragon in 1478 and its royal chapel holds the remains of the city's conqueror Ferdinand III of Castile, his son and heir Alfonso the Wise and their descendant king Peter the Just. Christopher Columbus and his son Diego are also buried in the cathedral. The Lagarto , or lizard (below right), actually a stuffed crocodile, which hangs from the ceiling in the corner of the Courtyard of the Oranges, and gives its name to the Gate of the Lizard , the old Moorish gate with the typical Visigothic horseshoe arch next to the Giralda Tower. When the Cathedral was constructed, the builders preserved some elements from the ancient mosque. The mosque's sahn , that is, the courtyard for ablutions for the faithful to conduct their ritual cleansing before entering the prayer hall is known today as the Patio de los Naranjos . It contains a fountain and orange trees. However, the most well known is its minaret, which was converted into a bell tower known as La Giralda , and is now the city's most well-known symbol. The Osborne Bull is a 14-metre high black silhouetted image of a bull in semi-profile. The large silhouette was originally designed to advertise a brandy, but over the years it's become an iconic symbol of Spain. There are at least 90 of them located outdoors all over the country.

title: France - 2013
text: France - 2013 St.Malo - November 2013 Brittany Ferries was offering a great deal for a 3-night trip to St.Malo from the ferry port in Plymouth. We boarded at night and had a comfortable cabin for the overnight trip - arriving into St.Malo early the following morning. Our hotel (Hotel de l'universe) was cheap and cheerful but very conveniently situated to explore the town. The hotel was directly opposite the city's impressive medieval castle, the Château de St Malo , which was once owned by the Dukes of Brittany. From the top of the château it is possible to see all over the town - including the Gothic and Romanesque Cathédrale de St Malo . Our first lunch stop with a cup of apple beer and a glass of chardonnay (plus pretzels) while we waited for our crêpes to arrive. After lunch we braved the cold and did some sightseeing, including a brisk walk along the sea walls. It was very cold in St.Malo but all restaurants had outdoor heaters and many had plastic canopies which successfully kept out the wind and rain - and which were mesmerising to watch in the wind. Up early for our trip home and we saw our ferry in the early morning light. That was the best of the weather as it closed in and was fairly choppy for the trip back across the Channel.

title: Venice - 1979
text: Venice - 1979 Venice - August 1979 Back in Summer 1979, after my first year at university, a group of us took a mini-bus to Italy - stopping off in Asti, Cuneo, Florence, Venice, Urbino, Piacenza and Pisa. It was dark when we arrived at our campsite in Venice, so it was only the next morning that we discovered we were staying next to a sulphur dioxide plant ...! The quality of my instamatic camera left a lot to be desired - but it did at least record that I was there. The Grand Canal always looks impressive, even if slightly out of focus. Yours truly posing before a visit to the Doge's Palace and taking the obligatory photo from the Bridge of Sighs (below).

title: Venice - 2010
text: Venice - 2010 Venice - April 2010 After 31 years, it was time to return to Venice - this time to celebrate my 50th birthday. We took a vaporetto (water bus) down the Grand Canal to reaquaint ourselves with the layout of Venice The Rialto Bridge is the oldest of the four bridges spanning the Grand Canal. Connecting the sestieri (districts) of San Marco and San Polo, it has been rebuilt several times since its first construction as a pontoon bridge in 1173. The present stone bridge, a single span designed by Antonio da Ponte, was built between 1588 and 1591. On either side of the portico, the covered ramps carry rows of shops. The engineering of the bridge was considered so audacious that architect Vincenzo Scamozzi predicted future ruin. The bridge has defied its critics to become one of the architectural icons of Venice. At Saint Mark's Square , we took another vaporetto out to the Lido . Back then to the water around Saint Mark's Square to the vaporetto station and then a visit to the Doge's Palace. The Doge's Palace is built in Venetian Gothic style and was the residence of the Doge of Venice, the supreme authority of the former Republic. It was built in 1340, extended and modified in the following centuries and it became a museum in 1923. When we visited part of the façade was covered up due to restoration work. In 1485, the Great Council of Venice decided that a ceremonial staircase should be built within the Palace courtyard. Since 1567, the Giants’ Staircase has been guarded by Sansovino's two colossal statues of Mars and Neptune, which represent Venice’s power by land and by sea, and the reason for its name. Members of the Senate gathered before government meetings in the Senators' Courtyard, to the right of the Giants’ Staircase. The Bridge of Sighs ( Ponte dei Sospiri ) connects the New Prison ( Prigioni Nuove ) to the interrogation rooms in the Doge's Palace. It was designed and built in 1600 by Antonio Contino, whose uncle Antonio da Ponte designed the Rialto Bridge. The view from the Bridge of Sighs was allegedly the last view of Venice that convicts saw before their imprisonment. The bridge's English name was bequeathed by Lord Byron in the 19th century as a translation from the Italian from the suggestion that prisoners would sigh at their final view of beautiful Venice through the window before being taken down to their cells. Below is the same obligatory photograph that I had taken in 1979. A trip out to the islands on the Venetian Lagoon. The first stop was at the Isola di San Michele , Venice's cemetery. Along with the neighbouring island of San Cristoforo, it was selected to become a cemetery in 1807 when, under French occupation, it was decreed that burial on the main Venetian islands was unsanitary. The canal that separated the two islands was filled in during 1836, and subsequently the larger island became known as San Michele. Bodies were carried to the island on special funeral gondolas. Among those buried there are Igor Stravinsky, Sergei Diaghilev and Ezra Pound. The cemetery is still in use today although disappointingly closed on the day when we tried to visit. The next stop, Murano , was made up of seven islands, linked by bridges over eight channels. It has a reputation as the centre for glassmaking. In the 13th century, many of Venice’s buildings were made of wood. Glass factories at this time would often catch fire and the Venetian Republic feared the devastation of their city and ordered all glass furnaces to be moved to the nearby island of Murano. It is now a tourist trap and we didn't delay here too long. Burano is known for its small, brightly painted houses, which follow a specific system. The idea was so that fisherman in the village would recognise their houses in the fog, which is prevalent during early hours much of the year. The island is also known for lacemaking. . And finally to Torcello . In pre-Medieval times, Torcello was a much more powerful trading centre than Venice. Thanks to the lagoon’s saline marshes, salt became Torcello’s economic backbone and its harbour developed quickly into an important re-export market. However the Black Death devastated the area of Venice and all the nearby islands, and Torcello was a bigger problem due to the swamp area that completely surrounds the island; malaria was greatly aggravated as well. Navigation in the laguna morta (dead lagoon) was impossible before long and traders ceased coming. As a result, the population dwindled and even the bishop transferred to Murano, leaving only a few people behind. . Torcello was the bishop’s official seat for more than a thousand years. Visitors brought with them the relics of Saint Heliodorus, now the patron saint of the island. It was first settled in the year 452 and has been referred to as the parent island from which Venice was populated. Locanda Cipriani is still owned by the family who run Harry's Bar. Simple but world-famous it was where we came for my 50th birthday lunch which was extremely memorable. San Giorgio Maggiore is one of the islands of Venice, lying south of the main island group. The island is now best known for the Church of San Giorgio Maggiore , designed by Palladio and begun in 1566. The belltower has a ring of 9 bells in C#. In the early 19th century, after the Republic fell, the island became a free port with a new harbour built in 1812. It became the home of Venice's artillery. It has been much painted, featuring for example in a series by Monet and also contains several paintings by, amongst others, Jacopo Tintoretto. San Giorgio Maggiore at Dusk - Claude Monet 1908–1912 The Jews in the Desert - Jacopo Tintoretto 1593 The Last Supper - Jacopo Tintoretto 1592-94 We climbed the campanile (bell tower) of the church and enjoyed glorious views over the whole of Venice and the lagoon. The large bell started ringing while we were up the tower. It was very loud! Santa Maria della Salute , commonly known simply as the Salute , is a minor basilica which stands on the narrow finger of Punta della Dogana, between the Grand Canal and the Giudecca Canal. In 1630, Venice experienced an unusually devastating outbreak of the plague. As a votive offering for deliverance from the pestilence, the Republic of Venice vowed to build and dedicate a church to Our Lady of Health. Construction began in 1631. Many of the objects of art housed in the church bear references to the Black Death. Back in Saint Mark's Square, the crowds were diminishing at the end of a busy day, so it was now possible to admire the façade of the Doge's Palace and to see the famous Venetian winged lions. The Basilica di Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari , usually just called the Frari , is one of the most prominent churches in the city. It has the status of a minor basilica and is dedicated to the Assumption of Mary. The interior contains a Bellini altarpiece and works by Titian and Donatello and is notable for many grand monuments to distinguished Venetians who are buried in the church, including the sculptor Canova, the composer Monteverdi and the painter Titian. Madonna and Child with Ss. Nicholas of Bari, Peter, Mark and Benedict - Giovanni Bellini 1488 The Pesaro Madonna - Titian 1519–1526 and St. John the Baptist - Donatello 1438 Venice has its own opera house - the Teatro La Fenice. We spent the rest of the afternoon getting lost in the muddle of walkways, bridges and canals. We were amused to see several gondoliers having a sleep in their gondolas . The Chiesa di San Moisè was built initially in the 8th century. It is dedicated to Moses since like the Byzantines, the Venetians often considered Old Testament prophets as canonised saints. It also honours Moisè Venier, the aristocrat who funded the reconstruction. The elaborate Baroque facade, dating from 1668, is profusely decorated with sculpture, including a bust of its patron, Vincenzo Fini, which is found over the entry door. title: Ventimiglia - 1987
text: Ventimiglia - 1987 Ventimiglia - August 1987 A trip to Italy for the wedding of my old school friend, Jonathan Glanz, to Manuela Raimondo whom he met on holiday in the Maldives. Friends Sarah Buttleman, Rob Hume, Jack Jacouvou, Stephen McDougall, Ian Giddons and Jon's sister Lesley and her husband Mike all flew out to attend the wedding. We stayed in Bordighera, the next town along the coast from Ventimiglia, where the wedding was to take place at the Town Hall. Other friends (Bernadette and David) and Manuela's relatives (including her brother Vittorio) joined us on the morning of the wedding itself - along with Vita (Jon's relation from Paris) and her pal Ado. The ceremony itself was surprisingly informal: the Notary, wearing a sash jauntily around his waist, talked us through the details while best man Sarah, 'natta a Ilford' , provided the rings. We then moved outside for confetti and the usual photographs. All of us then walked down to the seafront to a rather wonderful restaurant where the 'wedding breakfast' and speeches took place. It was baking hot so shirt-sleeves were the order of the day.

title: Ventimiglia - 1988
text: Ventimiglia - 1988 Ventimiglia - August 1988 The following year, 1988, I returned to Ventimiglia and this time stayed in Manuela's flat which was only five minutes from the beach. Here we are waiting for some home-made croissants to be cooked for breakfast. The view from the kitchen window was of other balconies with the ubiquitous green canopies. We took a bus one day up to Dolceacqua - a pretty village up in the hills in the 'Ligurian hinterland'. Ventimiglia's beach was just at the end of the road from Manuela's apartment. It was a pebbly beach but very clean and the water was clear and very safe in which to swim. Jon and Manuela came out to Ventimiglia (I think they must have stayed with her parents, Dino and Bruna, as we didn't have to move out of her apartment) and they took us up into the Ligurian hills above the town. Returning into town, it was all too much for Ian who promptly dozed off ... Another day we took the train to Turin and, as luck would have it, the Turin Shroud was on display. Some claim the image depicts Jesus of Nazareth and the fabric is the burial shroud in which he was wrapped after crucifixion. First mentioned in 1354, the shroud was denounced in 1389 by the local bishop of Troyes as a fake. Currently the Catholic Church neither formally endorses nor rejects the shroud, and in 2013 Pope Francis referred to it as an “icon of a man scourged and crucified”. The shroud has been kept in the royal chapel of the Cathedral of Turin since 1578. Our final jaunt away from Ventimiglia took us over the border to Nice in France where we visited the Cemetery at the Monastère de Cimiez and had a fine lunch in the centre of old Nice.

title: Ventimiglia - 1993
text: Ventimiglia - 1993 Ventimiglia - August 1993 A return trip to Ventimiglia, this time in August 1993, with friends Ian and Danny. As you can see, we flew from Stansted airport. Back in Manuela's apartment, everything was comfortingly the same, even if the residents this time were different and moodier. The morning routine of baking croissants remained consistent too. As my spoken Italian was more-or-less non-existent, Ian insisted on giving me a lesson in pronunciation which seemed to involve me clenching my teeth ... And then to the beach which was only five minutes away - and there were several really nice restaurants along the sea-front, which we had to try (naturally) ... A bus trip up into the hills took us to the pretty village of Dolceacqua . After a heavy day sight-seeing, it was back down to the beach for another swim before supper. Ian had to return early to England, so we spent his last morning having a mooch around 'old' Ventimiglia and then a final lunch. While in the 'old' town we noticed posters for 'Medieval Ventimiglia' events which were to commence that evening. We returned in the evening to see the historical procession of the Sestieri - rival groups and clans all dressed in brightly-coloured tunics and carrying matching flags which they whirled around and threw to each other in a spectacular candle-lit display. Danny and I then took a train trip to Genoa - to see the Cathedral and tour the city. English National Opera were performing Verdi's Simon Boccanegra later that season and I managed the singer who would portray the title role, so it was particularly pleasing to track down some proof that the character actually existed. It was Ascension Day in Italy and all banks were closed. The restaurant where we had lunch did not take credit cards and we were in a bit of a pickle as we didn't have enough cash to pay the bill. Eventually, after a nerve-wracking two hours, the ATM nearby finally chugged into life and spat out some cash at us - hence Danny's excitement ... Chiesa S. Maria della Vigne. Our final day in Ventimiglia before we had to return to Nice Airport to catch the plane home.

title: Ventimiglia - 2000
text: Ventimiglia - 2000 Ventimiglia - August 2000 Another visit to Ventimiglia, this time with my friend Marion. After a quick flit around town, we took the bus up to the nearby pretty village Dolceacqua where we had a delicious lunch. Back for supper in the flat and the local char lady came in to do the washing-up! Another day we took the bus to the Villa Hanbury which was established by Sir Thomas Hanbury who purchased the extant Palazzo Orengo property in 1867 and, over decades, created the garden with the aid of pharmacologist Daniel Hanbury (his brother) and landscape designer Ludwig Winter. In 1912 the Hortus Mortolensis , the catalogue of the garden, contained 5,800 species, although the garden itself had more. Back to the apartment for a quick change (and a 'fist' of the Pringles) and then out for a pizza and some serious postcard writing. I never could work out why I posed with a rock on my head - possibly to stop my hat blowing off ...? Given that Marion and I had met through ballroom dancing, it was apt that we found an afternoon tea-dancing club where we went and danced with some lovely old locals. Marion's fan came in handy. Our final evening was spent with Manuela's parents in an excruciatingly hot Chinese restaurant (no air-con). The food was pretty awful and we couldn't really understand each other which was a shame. Here we are toasting each other with some Chinese whisky.

title: Ventimiglia - 2002
text: Ventimiglia - 2002 Ventimiglia - October 2002 Another visit to Ventimiglia - this time in October (I had always been in high Summer in the past) and the weather was noticeably cooler and many of the tourist restaurants had closed for the season. However, we did have a couple of days when the temperature was still plenty warm enough to sit on the beach and eat out at lunchtime. Another visit to the Villa Hanbury - and this time we explored the succulent garden, including some marvellous Agaves, Dasylirions and Cycads. Another visit to Dolceaqua - this time in the rain. We took a train trip up to Turin and went to Turin Cathedral and also found the magnificent National Museum of Cinema which is housed in the Mole Antonelliana , named after its architect, Alessandro Antonelli. A mole in Italian is a building of monumental proportions. Construction began in 1863, soon after Italian unification, and was completed in 1889, after the architect's death. Originally conceived as a synagogue, it now houses the Cinema Museum, and is believed to be the tallest museum in the world.

title: Vienna - 1994
text: Vienna - 1994 Vienna - February 1994 A work trip to Vienna's Konzerthaus for Handel's Jephtha with Lynne Dawson as Iphis. I was accompanied by my pal Isabel Murphy whom I worked with back in English National Opera days. After the work stuff was out of the way, Isabel and I were free to explore Vienna. We visited the Karlskirche (St.Charles Church) , considered the most outstanding baroque church in Vienna, as well as one of the city's greatest buildings. The church is dedicated to Saint Charles Borromeo, one of the great counter-reformers of the sixteenth century. It was built in 1713, one year after the last great plague epidemic, by Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor, who pledged to build a church for his namesake patron saint, Charles Borromeo, revered as a healer for plague sufferers. Outside the Vienna State Opera and choosing a new hair style! In the Stadtpark we found the gilded bronze monument of Johann Strauss II, is one of the most known and most frequently photographed monuments in Vienna. It was unveiled to the public on 26 June 1921 and is framed by a marble relief made by Edmund Hellmer. The gilding was removed in 1935 and laid on again only in 1991 - so was still fairly dazzling when we saw it. Back into the centre - we were pretty tired by this point - and we retired to our hotel for supper. The next day we set off again to visit the Stephansdom (St.Stephen's Cathedral) - the mother church of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Vienna. The current Romanesque and Gothic form of the cathedral, seen today in the Stephansplatz, was largely initiated by Duke Rudolf IV (1339–1365) and stands on the ruins of two earlier churches. With its multi-coloured tile roof, it has become one of the city's most recognisable symbols. The Haas-House is at the Stock-im-Eisen-Platz. Designed by the Austrian architect Hans Hollein, it is in the post-modernist style and was completed in 1990. The use of the Haas-Haus is divided between retail and a restaurant. The building is controversial owing to its contrast with the adjacent Stephansdom cathedral. The Prater is a large public park in Vienna's Second district (Leopoldstadt). The Wurstelprater, an amusement park, lies in one corner of the Wiener Prater and includes the Wiener Riesenrad Ferris Wheel which feaures in Carol Reed's 1949 film The Third Man starring Joseph Cotten and Orson Welles. The name Prater derives from one of two Latin words: 'pratum' meaning meadow and 'Praetor' meaning magistrate or lawyer.

title: 1.Arrival
text: Florida - 1997 Gander - Newfoundland . Our 11-hour flight to Orlando had to be diverted to Gander in Newfoundland, Canada because of bad weather. We were allowed to disembark and explore the very retro airport terminal but the only thing to buy was some random postcards (illustrated), some smoked meat and bottles of the local Newfoundland rum called 'Screech'.

title: 2.Key West
text: Florida - 1997 Key West Collecting a hire-car from Orlando airport, and after a mistaken diversion 30 miles to the north which necessitated an overnight stop at a motel, we drove down the Florida Keys and arrived into Key West on Christmas Eve 1997. Christmas lunch consisted of shrimps, oysters and lobster - followed by a swim in the pool of our guest house.

title: 3.Dry Tortugas
text: Florida - 1997 Dry Tortugas A day-long boat trip took us to the Dry Tortugas, a small group of islands, located in the Gulf of Mexico about 67 miles (108 km) west of Key West. The first Europeans to discover the islands were the Spanish in 1513, led by explorer Juan Ponce de León. The archipelago's name derives from the lack of fresh water springs, and the presence of turtles. The major structure on the Dry Tortugas is Fort Jefferson, a massive but unfinished coastal fortress. It is the largest brick masonry structure in the Americas and is composed of over 16 million bricks and covers 16 acres. T his bastion remained in Union hands throughout the Civil War and was later used as a prison until abandoned in 1874. Dr.Samuel Mudd, famous for being the doctor who treated John Wilkes Booth in the wake of the Lincoln assassination, was imprisoned here until early 1869. During the 1880s, the Navy established a base in the Dry Tortugas, and it subsequently set up a coaling (refueling) and a wireless (radio) station there as well. During World War I, a seaplane base was established in the islands, but it was abandoned soon thereafter.

title: 4.Florida Keys
text: Florida - 1997 Florida Keys Driving back north from Key West, we saw the full aspect of t he Florida Keys, a coral cay archipelago forming the southernmost part of the continental United States. One of the longest bridges when it was built, the Seven Mile Bridge, connects Knight's Key (part of the city of Marathon in the Middle Keys) to Little Duck Key in the Lower Keys. The piling-supported concrete bridge is 6.79 miles (10.93 km) long. The current bridge bypasses Pigeon Key (above) a small island that housed workers building Florida's East Coast Railway in the 1900s, that the original Seven Mile Bridge crossed. A short section of the old bridge remains for access to the island, although it was subsequently closed to vehicular traffic in 2008. Much of the vegetation of the Florida Keys is mangrove swamp. Despite this being a tourist destination we found very few restaurants of any significant quality and had to resort to cooking our own food on a BBQ at our motel. Neither of us I think would make it to the final of Master Chef on the basis of this particular meal ...

title: 5.Miami
text: Florida - 1997 Miami Arriving into Miami the first thing we noticed on the beach were the number and variety of lifeguard huts. Many were painted in bold colours and took their inspiration from the Art Deco buildings fronting South Beach . In the 1930s, an architectural revolution came to South Beach, bringing Art Deco architecture and giving it a legitimate claim to have the world's largest collection of Streamline Moderne Art Deco architecture. Napier, New Zealand, another notable Art Deco city, is architecturally comparable to Miami Beach as it was rebuilt in the Ziggurat Art Deco style after being destroyed by an earthquake in 1931. While many of the unique Art Deco buildings, such as the New Yorker Hotel, were lost to developers in the years before 1980, the area was saved as a cohesive unit by Barbara Baer Capitman and a group of activists who spearheaded the movement to place almost one square mile of South Beach on the National Register of Historic Places. We first checked into this iconic building but quickly checked out again when we discovered cockroaches in the bathroom. We did however retain our parking card (223) so we were able to have free parking for the time we spent in the city! On New Year's Eve 1997 we had lunch at the Delano Hotel, Philippe Starck's minimalist redesign of architect Robert Swartburg's 1947 structure. The hotel was originally utilised for military housing and its four-winged Art Deco tower was then the tallest building in Miami. The hotel is named after US President Franklin Delano Roosevelt. That evening found us at Escuelita - a fabulous gay salsa and merengue venue. We sat a table marked 'reserved' for much of the evening but, at ten minutes to midnight, a party of outrageous characters (drag queens, an ex Miss Venezuela etc) arrived and the handsome party leader asked if we could move, but could he buy us a drink to say thank you. He was Enrique Iglesias ... We danced all night, won a lifelong membership to the club in a raffle (it closed two years after we were there so it wouldn't have done us any good) and then retired to Wolfie's deli (as featured in Elmore Leonard's novel Rum Punch ) for a slap-up breakfast and to soak up the alcohol. The New Year's Day Rose Bowl parade was a particularly sparkly affair and we found assorted kitsch features to enhance the day. Finally we stopped at Casa Casuarina, Gianni Versace's opulent mansion where he was gunned down by his lover. In a remarkable lapse of taste, I posed dead on the steps of the mansion before being moved on by an armed policeman who wasn't amused ... Despite the flippancy above, we did see a lot of poverty and deprivation in this superficially glossy party town.

title: 6.Everglades
text: Florida - 1997 Everglades Leaving Miami and driving along what is known as 'Alligator Alley' (Interstate 75), we entered Everglades National Park, a natural region of tropical wetlands comprising the southern half of a large drainage basin which begins near Orlando and which discharges into the vast but shallow Lake Okeechobee. The Seminole Tribe gave the large body of water the name Okeechobee meaning 'River of Grass' to describe the sawgrass marshes, part of a complex system of interdependent ecosystems that include cypress swamps, the estuarine mangrove forests of the Ten Thousand Islands, tropical hardwood hammocks, pine rockland and the marine environment of Florida Bay. The park is the largest tropical wilderness in the United States, and the largest wilderness of any kind east of the Mississippi River . Thirty-six threatened or protected species inhabit the park, including the Florida panther, the American crocodile, and the West Indian manatee, along with 350 species of birds, 300 species of fresh and saltwater fish, 40 species of mammals, and 50 species of reptiles .

title: 7.Tampa
text: Florida - 1997 Tampa Arriving in Tampa, we visited the historic Tampa Film Theatre and watched Atom Egoyan's The Sweet Hereafter with Ian Holm, an art film unusual for a venue such as this. You can't beat a straight-out bonkers keyboard player. Tampa's very own female version of Doctor John (albeit it only playing in a car park) ... Created in 1947 by stunt swimmer and attraction promoter Newt Perry, who based the show on underwater air-hose breathing techniques, "Weeki Wachee Springs" was first named by Seminole Indians, which means 'Little Spring' or 'Winding River' in their language. First an 18-seat theatre, then later a newer theatre with a capacity of 50, which was embedded in the lime rock of the spring with viewing windows below the surface of the water, to allow visitors to watch the mermaids perform in the water. The brown pelican ( Pelecanus occidentalis ) is a North American bird of the pelican family, Pelecanidae . It is one of three pelican species found in the Americas and one of two that feed by diving in water. It is found on the Atlantic Coast from Nova Scotia to the mouth of the Amazon River, and along the Pacific Coast from British Columbia to northern Chile, including the Galapagos Islands.

title: 1.A Touch Of Murder
text: I, Claudius 1. A TOUCH OF MURDER Rome, 24 - 23 BC Emperor Augustus begins to favour his nephew Marcellus over his old friend and ally Agrippa, who leaves Rome in protest. Livia wants her son Tiberius to become Augustus' heir, so she secretly poisons Marcellus, who eventually dies. Augustus has Agrippa return to Rome and, to seal their renewed friendship, he gives his daughter Julia, Marcellus' widow, to Agrippa to be his wife, infuriating Livia, who wanted Julia to marry Tiberius to cement his status as Augustus' heir. title: 2.Family Affairs
text: I, Claudius 2. FAMILY AFFAIRS Rome, 9 BC Nine years have passed. Agrippa is dead and Tiberius has been forced to marry Julia, divorcing Vipsania Agrippina. Still deeply in love, he continues to meet Vipsania secretly, enraging Augustus, but Livia defends him by claiming that he had informed her of the meetings. Tiberius is briefly comforted by the presence of his brother Drusus, who quarrels with Livia before leaving once again on campaign. Drusus soon writes to Tiberius, asking for his brother's help in convincing Augustus to retire and return Rome to a Republic, but the letter is intercepted and read by both Livia and Augustus. Drusus falls from his horse and crushes his leg, and his condition worsens under the oversight of Livia's personal physician. He dies in the presence of his wife, Antonia, and their recently-born son Claudius. Augustus looks forward to sharing his power with his grandsons Lucius and Gaius when they come of age. title: 3.Waiting In The Wings
text: I, Claudius 3. WAITING IN THE WINGS Rome, AD 3 - 5 Gaius has died and Tiberius has been banished to Rhodes for his mistreatment of Julia. One day in the garden, the young Claudius catches a wolf cub dropped from an eagle's claws, leading the seer Thrasyllus of Mendes to predict that he will protect Rome in an hour of need. Livia's scheming continues: knowing of the mutual attraction between Livilla and Postumus Agrippa, she arranges their betrothal to other people; she enlists Lucius' friend Plautius as a spy against Julia, and tricks Lucius into revealing Julia's infidelities; a grief-stricken Augustus banishes her from Rome. The death of Lucius in a boating accident ends Tiberius' exile and he returns to Rome to be named, along with Postumus, as co-heir to Augustus' throne. title: 4.What Shall We Do About Claudius
text: I, Claudius 4. WHAT SHALL WE DO ABOUT CLAUDIUS? Rome, AD 9 Three Roman legions have been massacred in Germania at the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest. Tiberius and Germanicus are dispatched to exact revenge. While Claudius is in the library researching his family's history he is advised by Pollio, the historian, to play up his infirmities to enhance his place in his family as a harmless fool, and thus no threat to anyone. Augustus has determined that Postumus will succeed him as Emperor, but Livia overhears this. She tells Livilla she knows of her affair with Postumus and that during the Republic there was civil war and that a single ruler is needed to bring peace, so the succession can't be disputed. With Livilla's help, Postumus is framed for rape. Postumus tells Augustus Livia has been killing those who could prevent Tiberius succeeding but is not believed. Before he is banished, Postumus tells Claudius his (correct) suspicions of all the people whom Livia has killed and reiterates the advice that Claudius should continue to play the fool. The episode ends with his marriage to Plautia Urgulanilla, who is so much taller than Claudius that he becomes the butt of his family's uproarious, mocking laughter at their wedding. title: 5.Poison Is Queen
text: I, Claudius 5. POISON IS QUEEN Rome, AD 13 - 14 Germanicus has defeated the Germans and returns to Rome in triumph. Claudius tells him of Postumus' suspicions and Germanicus passes this information on to Augustus. On a trip to Corsica, Augustus stops to see Postumus and, now aware of Postumus' innocence, promises to pardon him. Augustus privately thanks Claudius for his role in opening his eyes, and informs him that he has already changed his will to favour Postumus. Livia, ever suspicious, tricks a Vestal Virgin into letting her inspect the revised will. Soon afterwards Augustus falls ill. He recovers slightly when he begins to eat only food that he has grown himself and picked by hand, but his recovery is short lived, the implication being that Livia poisons Augustus' figs while they still ripen on the vine. A Praetorian officer, Sejanus, is dispatched to kill Postumus and Tiberius prepares to take over as Emperor, being left two thirds of Augustus' property while Livia takes the remaining third. title: 6.Some Justice
text: I, Claudius 6. SOME JUSTICE Rome, AD 19 - 20 Tiberius, with Sejanus' help, is ruling with an iron fist. Only Germanicus is preventing total tyranny, but when he dies in Syria under mysterious circumstances, it is widely rumoured that Tiberius is behind it. Germanicus' wife Agrippina accuses Piso and his wife Plancina of murder and treason. At Claudius' suggestion, they are tried in the Senate, so as to avoid any backroom subversion of the courts by Tiberius' agents. Martina, the poisoner, is held in a secret location before the trial by Herod Agrippa and Claudius, but she is found by Livia's agents. She reveals to Livia that Germanicus' own son, Caligula, aided her in bringing about his death by convincing him that he had been cursed. Piso blackmails Livia and Tiberius with evidence that they approved of Germanicus' murder; Livia retaliates by threatening Plancina with Martina's testimony. Plancina attempts to convince Piso to commit suicide, knowing that she will be spared by such an outcome. When Piso has second thoughts, Plancina stabs him, bringing the trial to an end, and Agrippina and her friends have to be satisfied that at least "some justice" was done. title: 7.Queen Of Heaven
text: I, Claudius 7. QUEEN OF HEAVEN Rome, AD 23 - 29 Tiberius now only lives for his perversions, in which Caligula is only too happy to join. Sejanus oversees continual treason trials of notable citizens, and sleeps with Livilla, who becomes so enamoured of him that she poisons her husband Castor to be able to marry Sejanus. Sejanus manipulates Claudius into marrying his adopted sister Aelia, after telling him his first wife is pregnant by another man. Anticipating her coming death, Livia reveals to Claudius that an unpublished Sibylline prophecy claims that both he and Caligula will one day become Emperor, and makes each of them promise to make her a goddess so she can escape torment for her many misdeeds. Claudius agrees, on the condition that she reveal to him the full scope of her crimes. On her deathbed she receives a visit from Caligula, who rescinds his promise and reveals that he plans to become the greatest god the world has ever known. title: 8.Reign Of Terror
text: I, Claudius 8. REIGN OF TERROR Rome, AD 30 - 31 Tiberius has retired to Capri. Sejanus consolidates his hold on power in Rome by engineering the banishment of Agrippina and her son Nero and having her other son Drusus arrested. Sejanus has divorced his wife Apicata and approaches Tiberius about marrying Livilla. Tiberius refuses as the marriage would mean Sejanus would be elevated in rank but suggests that he could marry Livilla's daughter Helen. An outraged Livilla attempts to poison Helen. Antonia discovers letters from her daughter to Sejanus, implicating them both in several deaths and urging Sejanus to murder Tiberius. Claudius smuggles the evidence to Tiberius. At Caligula's suggestion, Tiberius orders Macro to execute Sejanus, his followers, and his family, including Claudius' wife. Meanwhile Antonia locks Livilla in her room and says she will stay there until she dies. title: 9.Zeus By Jove
text: I, Claudius 9. ZEUS, BY JOVE! Rome, AD 37 - 38 Tiberius dies (actually smothered to death by Macro with Caligula's connivance), leaving Caligula and his cousin, Gemellus (son of Livilla), as his joint heirs. Claudius' lifelong friend Herod has returned to Rome in time for Caligula's ascension. Caligula chooses Claudius to be his co-consul, over Claudius' objections. Caligula displays signs of mental instability and falls into a coma; upon awakening he declares that he has become Zeus. Claudius humours him, hoping that Caligula will reveal his divinity to the Senate and be deposed, restoring the Republic; instead, the Senate accepts Caligula's claims of divinity. Caligula becomes increasingly violent: Lentulus, a Senator who told Macro during Caligula's coma he would give his life if Caligula lived, is forced to commit suicide; Caligula also has Gemellus killed. He declares his sister Drusilla his wife. Disgusted with the depths of depravity that her family and Rome have sunk to, Antonia commits suicide. Fearing that his child will become greater than he, Caligula tries to recreate the birth of Athena: as Zeus reportedly did with Hera, Caligula cuts his unborn child from his sister's belly and eats it. title: 10.Hail Who
text: I, Claudius 10. HAIL WHO? Rome, AD 40 - 41 Claudius is living with the ex-prostitute Calpurnia in meagre circumstances. Caligula has turned the palace into a brothel where he sells the wives of high-ranking Senate members to the highest bidder during sexual orgies and forces Claudius to take money at the door. As a joke, he arranges for Claudius to marry the much younger, extremely beautiful Messalina. Totally insane, Caligula makes his horse, Incitatus, a senator and takes his legions on a campaign to Germany to put down an alleged rebellion and then to the English Channel where he attempts to do battle with Neptune, bringing back seashells as booty. Returning to Rome, he attempts to execute the entire Senate for not awarding him a Triumph for his 'victory', but his wife Caesonia and Claudius convince him not to. Cassius Chaerea, a leading Praetorian officer whom the Emperor continuously mocks, forms a plan with several others to assassinate Caligula. They strike during the games held to celebrate Augustus, luring him away from his German Guards and killing him. Cassius proceeds to murder Caligula's wife Caesonia and their infant daughter, Julia Drusilla, attempting to wipe out the Imperial family once and for all. While the, suddenly leaderless, Praetorian Guard are looting the palace, they come upon Claudius, hiding behind a curtain, and proclaim him Emperor over Claudius' protestations. title: 11.Fools Luck
text: I, Claudius 11. FOOL'S LUCK Rome, AD 41 - 43 The leaders of the Praetorian Guard and Herod convince Claudius that he should take up the Imperial crown, since the alternative would mean the death of his family. Claudius in turn convinces the Senate to proclaim him Emperor. In his first act, he condemns Cassius for the murder of Caesonia, but pardons the other conspirators. Livia is finally deified and made a goddess. After successfully bearing Claudius children, Messalina convinces him to share the burdens of power with her. As Herod will soon be leaving to take control of the lands in the East that Claudius has granted him, Messalina suggests that Appius Silanus, a Senator, be brought in to assist her husband. Later her mother Domitia and Silanus marry. Before Herod leaves he warns Claudius that, as Emperor, Claudius must trust no one, not his advisors, not his wife, not even Herod himself. Messalina attempts to seduce Silanus and tells him that Claudius approves, being just as corrupt as the Emperors who preceded him. Silanus then attempts to kill Claudius in the hopes of ending the line of depraved rulers. Messalina, with her mother's help, convinces Claudius of her own innocence and Silanus is put to death. title: 12.A God In Colchester
text: I, Claudius 12. A GOD IN COLCHESTER Rome, AD 47 - 48 Claudius is leading his troops in an invasion of Britain. Messalina's sexual excesses lead her to challenge the well-known prostitute Scylla to a contest to see who can take the most men in an evening; she wins easily. Claudius returns in triumph, and learns that Herod has organized a rebellion in the eastern provinces against his rule. Herod believes that he is the "King of the Jews", but he dies before completing his plans. Messalina takes Gaius Silius as her lover, and they divorce their respective spouses and marry, thinking that Rome will rally around them and proclaim them rulers. Forced to act, Claudius' servants Pallas and Narcissus enlist Calpurnia to tell the Emperor the truth. In the end he believes them and the conspirators are arrested and killed; a drunken Claudius even carelessly signs Messalina's execution order. As Claudius is mourning the fact that all whom he cared for are gone, he learns that the Britons have dedicated a temple to him in Colchester making him a god. title: 13.Old King Log
text: I, Claudius 13. OLD KING LOG Rome, AD 54 Claudius' benevolent rule of Rome leads the populace to accepting an emperor, but Claudius feels that this was a mistake. He decides that Rome must come to hate its ruling family, overthrow it, and restore the Republic. To do this, he marries his niece Agrippinilla and adopts her son Nero, making him co-heir with his son Britannicus. Because of a prophecy, Claudius knows that Nero will become the next ruler of Rome, but he still tries to protect Britannicus by planning to send him to Britain so that he may take over later when Nero dies; unfortunately, Britannicus' sense of honour will not allow him to fall in with Claudius' plans and Claudius, knowing the ultimate future, must leave his son to his fate. Ready for his end, Claudius voluntarily eats a poisoned mushroom from his wife's fork and dies. Looking for Claudius' will, Agrippinilla and Nero come upon his autobiography and burn it. Lying on his bier, Claudius and the Sibyl, knowing that Britannicus, Agrippinilla and Nero will ultimately die violently, have a good laugh over the fact that he buried another copy of his book to be found later. Claudius is told that, though the Republic won't be restored, Nero will be last of the Claudians and the Emperors that follow mostly won't be as bad. title: 0.Itinerary
text: Kerala & Tamil Nadu - 2004 Kerala & Tamil Nadu - Dec 2003 / Jan 2004 t A flight to Trivandrum (via Doha in Qatar) took us straight to the hustle and bustle of South India. Taking a "computer cab" (ie: a man with a bit of paper) we hurtled the 100km or so from the airport to Varkala, narrowly avoiding elephants and camels to arrive at our accommodation - the Government Guest House on Christmas Eve 2003. to Click on any place on the white itinerary line for a direct link to that page - or click the forward and back arrows to navigate the site.

title: 1.Varkala
text: Kerala & Tamil Nadu - 2004 Varkala Government Guest Houses are run for the civil service so that employees would always have somewhere to stay, when on a work trip, which are cheaper than a hotel. In the quiet season they are let out to the public and are astonishingly good value for an albeit simple room. We booked this one in Varkala in the days before the internet and it took several phone calls from England to get through to someone who could speak English (many people in Kerala only speak Hindi or Malayalam). The phone calls probably cost more than the cost of the accommodation. Arriving on Christmas Eve, the caretaker tried to tell us that they were "fully booked", even though the place was deserted. We refused to move as there was no where else to go: I demanded to see the reservation book and we found our booking despite them having misspelled my name. The caretake grudgingly admitted his mistake and offered us egg curry (made by his mother) as a welcome placatory gesture .

title: 2.Alleppey
text: Kerala & Tamil Nadu - 2004 Alleppey A splendid train journey north and we arrive in Alleppey (Alappuzha), a pleasant market town surrounded by coconut plantations and built on the canals that service the coir industry of the backwaters. We find the usual mix of stalls selling fruit, vegetables, pots and pans and even a coffin shop plus the obligatory mounds of rubbish being picked at by crows. ! We also stopped at Mount Carmel Roman Catholic Latin Cathedral with its black and white graveyard and were able to watch a wedding take place and also climb the tower to get a view over the whole town. Later on we visited a weaving business and walked to the beach where we met a host of children who were pouring out of their school as it was the end of the school day. Several of them dragged us to the boats where their fathers worked as fishermen. Happy and welcoming people!

title: 3.Backwaters
text: Kerala & Tamil Nadu - 2004 Backwaters Fringing the coast of Kerala, and winding far inland, is a vast network of lagoons, lakes, rivers and canals. These backwaters are both the basis of a distinct lifestyle and a fascinating thoroughfare. Travelling by boat along the backwaters certainly proved to be one of the highlights of our visit. There were three crew on our boat: captain, cook and general dogsbody. We could swim from the boat and our delicious food was served under cover of its banana leaf canopy. ! To the casual eye, the spread of water hyacinth looks attractive but, in fact, this is dangerous as it spreads so prolifically that it now clogs many stretches of the water and causes great disruption for the boat operators. On our trip we visited a small village where we bought provisions for dinner - fruit, vegetables, fish and tapioca which was not the delicious pudding I remember from school. This was served with chilli flakes. ! Can there be anything more lovely than floating down this tranquil waterway in a boat decorated with Christmas stars - and welcoming the arrival of 2004? Absolutely heavenly ... !

title: 4.Aravukadu
text: Kerala & Tamil Nadu - 2004 Aravukadu We had asked our guide to take us to somewhere 'different'. A day's sailing took us far from Alleppey to a temple called Arivukadu ('Forest of Knowledge' ) - as it contains many educational institutions - and also Aravukadu ('Killing Place'). The Sreedevi Temple is the most renowned in South India and is located at Punnapra. There is a myth regarding the origin of the temple which says that the goddess Bhadrakali came into being in order to kill the cruel demon ( asura ) who tyrannically ruled the place. The spot reddened with the evil blood of the demon is called asurampuzha . The holy sword of the goddess, which killed the demon, is washed in the Temple pond nearby (but we never got to see it). . ! The Festival of Temple starts in the Malayalam month of “Meenum” for ten days. People from various parts of the state come to the Temple to witness the various Festivities and Programmes. Thiripidutham , (Holding of the Lighted Torch) is a very important offering in which thousands of devotees participate. On the tenth day of the Festival after the Deeparadhana , devotees take a dip in the Temple Pond and come before the temple in wet clothes. The Poojari gives a lighted torch to the devotees and they go round the Temple in Prathikshna . It is their belief that all their Prayers will be granted by performing this particular offering. . . ! On the way back to Alleppey we passed another religious site but the crew on the boat sadly couldn't tell us anything about it. On further investigation it turns out to be the black granite 11th century Karumadi Kuttan (literally ' boy from Karumady ') Buddha image. This is set just near the canal bank. Visited by the Dalai Lama in 1965, it was discovered in the 1930s by Sir Robert Bristow, a colonial British engineer. Currently the statue is under the protection of the Kerala State Government. The left side of the statue is missing and is subject to historical debate as to the reason for its partial destruction. We also saw some snake boats which partake in the annual Nehru Cup Snakeboat Race which occurs in August each year. Each boat is crewed by up to 100 rowers shaded by gleaming silk umbrellas. We were there in January so the boats were in storage.

title: 5.Cochin
text: Kerala & Tamil Nadu - 2004 Cochin Another train ride north to Ernakulam and then a ferry over to Cochin. Called the 'Queen of the Arabian Sea', Cochin (Kochi) was an important spice trading centre on the west coast of India from the 14th century onward, and maintained a trade network with Arab merchants from the pre-Islamic era. Occupied by the Portuguese in 1503, it was the first of the European colonies in colonial India. It remained the main seat of Portuguese India until 1530, when Goa was chosen instead. The most evocative view in Cochin are the 'Chinese Nets' which are fixed land installations with a net which is cantilevered with rocks. This way of fishing is unique to the area, as it was introduced by Chinese explorers who landed there in the 14th century. Indeed, one interpretation of the city name Kochi is ‘co-chin', meaning ‘like China'. . ! Kathakali is a Hindu performance art in the Malayalam-speaking region of Kerala. It is one of the major forms of classical Indian dance: a "story play" genre of art, but one distinguished by the elaborately colourful make-up, costumes and facemasks that the traditionally male actor-dancers wear. Kathakali's roots are unclear: the fully developed style of Kathakali originated around the 17th century, but its roots are in the temple and folk arts which are traceable to at least the 1st millennium AD. A Kathakali performance, like all classical dance arts of India, synthesises music, vocal performers, choreography and hand and facial gestures together to express ideas. However, Kathakali differs in that it also incorporates movements from ancient Indian martial arts and athletic traditions of South India. . ! Constructed in 1567, the Paradesi Synagogue is the oldest active synagogue in the Commonwealth of Nations and is one of seven synagogues of the Malabar Yehudan Jewish community. Paradesi is a word used in several Indian languages, and the literal meaning of the term is "foreigners" applied to the synagogue because it was built by Sephardic or Spanish-speaking Jews, some of them from families exiled in Aleppo, Safed and other West Asian localities. Its treasures include Belgian glass chandeliers, a brass-railed pulpit, the 10th-century copper plates of privileges given to Joseph Rabban (the earliest known Cochin Jew) and the floor of the synagogue is composed of hundreds of Chinese 18th-century, hand-painted porcelain tiles, each of which is unique and which featured in Salman Rushdie's novel The Moor's Last Sigh . The spice trading history of Cochin is still very apparent in the town today. Here we met some girls whose father was a nut trader. Also shown are some street scenes including one of a builder with rudimentary bamboo scaffolding and our delightful guest house where we stayed for several nights. !

title: 6.Thrissur
text: Kerala & Tamil Nadu - 2004 Thrissur Our final morning in Cochin was unsettled. There was a statewide transport strike of taxis and buses. Luckily we had used the same tuk-tuk driver during our stay in Cochin and he agreed to come very early to take us to Ernakulam station (despite facing possible sanctions) so we could catch our train to Thrissur. We arrived so early we were able to grab an Indian 'railway station breakfast'. ! . The Vadakkunnathan Temple is an ancient Hindu temple dedicated to Shiva: a classic example of the architectural style of Kerala which has monumental towers on all four sides and also a kuttambalam (an enclosed temple theatre). According to popular local lore, this is the first temple built by Parasurama, the sixth avatar of Vishnu. . The Thrissur Pooram is an annual Hindu temple festival which features elephants. It is held at the Vadakkunnathan Temple every year on the Pooram day - the day when the moon rises with the Pooram star in the Malayalam Calendar month of Medam. . ! The Pooram takes place in May each year so we missed it (the photos above are from the internet and indicate what happens at the Festival). I was feeling as sick as a proverbial ayurvedic parrot (I'd eaten something bad on our last night in Cochin) and got steadily worse throughout the day. We walked all the way (there still being a transport strike) to the Thrissur Archeological Museum (pictured below) where I thought I was going to die. I sat on the wall outside the Museum and, astonishingly, a little man who looked a bit like Biggles pulled up on a motorbike and offered me a lift. I climbed on, leaving Seán behind, and he took me back to the hotel. He returned and collected Seán, whom I was convinced I would never see again ... . ! The next day, having virtually spewed out my entire body weight, I felt much better and we travelled to our next stop - Coimbatore .

title: 7.Coimbatore
text: Kerala & Tamil Nadu - 2004 Coimbatore Coimbatore is a large business and industrial city known as either the Manchester or Detroit of the south for its textile manufacturing and engineering goods. While it doesn't hold any particular attraction for tourists, Coimbatore is a convenient overnight stop (although we didn't - we just went direct to the train station) for tourists heading up to Ooty or other Nilgiri hill stations. ! . We found a mass of stalls offering letter writing services either by hand or using a typewrite. Many of the inhabitants or people passing through would appear to be illiterate - hence the services offered. . We were also shocked at the levels of poverty on display in this relatively prosperous town. Above are shanties where people were living. . !

title: 8.Ooty
text: Kerala & Tamil Nadu - 2004 Ooty We hadn't booked ahead so could not take the Blue Mountain Railway train and, instead, had to take a cramped bus up to Ooty (Udhagamandalam). The railway is very pretty, taking seven years to build, finishing in 1898. Along its route are 13 tunnels, 19 bridges (see below) and 11 stations. Quite different from the toy trains found in places like Shimla and Darjeeling in northern India, the Blue Mountain train has a unique pinion rack system, with the locomotive pushing, rather than pulling, the carriages . . ! ! We stayed at the Nilgiri Woodlands Hotel, a Raj-era hotel which had seen better days. The place needed some maintenance and the plumbing was due for retirement but it had an alluring character and pretty manicured gardens. It also harboured unwelcome guests: we were awoken in the night by rats scuttling around under the floorboards of our chalet room. . ! We were promised unparalleled views of 'stunning wildlife' (gaurs, sambar deer, wild dogs, Malabar squirrels, langurs and bonnet macaques) so took a day-trip in a ricketty old mini-bus to Mudumalai National Park. On the way we stopped at some stunning scenic viewpoints which we were told were often used for Indian films - although we saw no evidence of this.. In fact the only wildlife we saw were some aggressive monkeys (one of which stole an orange) and the tail of something fleeing into the undergrowth. It was possibly the most uncomfortable bus I've ever been on (a real 'bone shaker') but nonetheless a memorable day out. Back in Ooty, we also visited St. Stephen's Church. Built in 1829, St. Stephen's is the oldest church in the Nilgiris. Its huge wooden beams came from the palace of Tipu Sultan in Srirangapatnam - they were hauled the 120km distance by a team of elephants. It was a quiet, peaceful place and the attached cemetery contained the graves of many early pioneers, including John Sullivan, the founder of Ooty.

title: 9.Madurai
text: Kerala & Tamil Nadu - 2004 Madurai From Ooty we took a taxi back down to Coimbatore (we couldn't face another uncomfortable bus ride) and, from there, we took the train to Madurai. Arriving almost an hour and a half early into Madurai at five in the morning we had to jump to it quickly to get all our stuff together and get off the train. Another Australian passenger got off so quickly that, once the train had departed, he discovered that he had left his passport and wallet on the train ... He spent the rest of the day at the Police Station reporting the loss of his documents. Disaster was averted when a humble cleaner - at the end of the line - discovered the passport and sent it back to Madurai on the next train. His honesty was astonishing as there was as much cash in the wallet as the cleaner probably earned in a month. . ! Designed in 1560 by Vishwanatha Nayak, the Sri Meenakshi Temple was substantially built during the reign of Tirumalai Nayak (1623-55) but its history goes back 2,000 years to the time when Madurai was the capital of the Pandya kings. The temple, a spectacular pastiche of Dravidian architecture, celebrates the enormously popular and powerful goddess Meenakshi who is the deity and protector of Madurai. Almost a city within a city, it features highly decorative gopurams and towers, and also columned halls such as the Kilikattu Mandapam as well as shops and, bizarrely, a warren of tailoring businesses. . ! We also met the friendly Temple elephant with her mahout. Her trick was to pick a coin from the head of a bystander with her trunk and pass it to the keeper . . ! As is often the case in religious establishments (and Hindu temples are no exception), it's an opportunity to rake in money from the weak-willed and / or faithful. At the Sri Meenakshi Temple, worshippers were encouraged to light candles made from ghee and purchase pats of rather rancid butter and fling them at a statue of the goddess Meenakshi. If the butter pat sticks to the statue this reputedly gives good luck. . ! We returned to the Temple at 9pm in the evening to watch the ceremony when the movable images of the god and goddess are carried to the bedchamber. Here the final puja ceremony of the day - the lalipuja - is performed, when for thirty minutes or so the priests sing lullabies ( lali ) before closing the Temple for the night. . ! Remember the guy who lost his passport and wallet? After it was returned to him he celebrated by taking us to the Apollo 96 , a crazy roof-top bar with a sci-fi theme - " boasting 75,000 flashing diodes " - Tamil Nadu's hi-tech bar looked just like the set of a low-budget 1970s movie ... . !

title: 10.Madurai2
text: Kerala & Tamil Nadu - 2004 Madurai We stayed at the Aarathy Hotel in Madurai. It overlooks the Kudalagar Temple and has a busy open-air restaurant that is especially popular when Mahalakshmi, the Temple elephant, is led through each morning and evening. . ! The Tirumalai Nayak Palace was built in 1636 and is about 1.5km from the Sri Meenakshi Temple. It was partly demolished by Tirumalai's grandson who wanted much of the fine structure (and associated jewels and woodcarvings) for his own palace at Trichy (but his dream was never realised). Today only the entrance gate, main hall and dance hall remain. Massive stone pillars support elegant cornices that give the roof of the palace a height of 20m. There is a daily sound-and-light show in English and Tamil when a few coloured lights are turned on and off and an audio cassette played at maximum volume. The text, interspersed with Tamil songs, is like Monty Python meets Shakespeare. Tickets are Rs 2 to 5 depending on whether you want a metal or plastic chair. . ! All that remains of the Rangavilasa (the palace where Tirumalai's brother Muthialu once lived) are ten pillars, wedged in a tiny back street appropriately named Ten Pillar South Lane. One pillar contains a shivalingam, worshipped by passers-by. We then continued on to the Flower and Textile Markets where we met some very friendly workers and I also had my hair-cut: the whole street came to watch ... . ! Street life in India is manic: noisy bustling tuk-tuks plying for trade, sacred cows foraging through discarded rubbish (broken neon tubes and other trash) for something to eat and people who extraordinarily make a living from collecting carbon paper (one of the lasting hang-overs from Imperial rule). If you get up early enough (about 5am) the overnight street sweepers have cleared everything away, but by breakfast time, the streets are filthy once again ... . !

title: 11.Padmanabhapuram
text: Kerala & Tamil Nadu - 2004 Padmanabhapuram Another train journey (to Trivandrum) and a visit back (by taxi) to the Padmanabhapuram Palace - once the seat of the rulers of the princely state of Travancore, which included a large part of present-day Kerala and the western coast of Tamil Nadu. The palace is superbly constructed of local teak and granite and stands within massive stone walls. The oldest parts of the palace date from AD 1550 . It was occupied from 1550 until 1790 when the then raja moved to Trivandrum. . ! Chinese traders sold tea and bought spice here for centuries and their legacy is evident throughout the palace. There are intricately carved rosewood chairs, screens and ceilings as well as large Chinese pickle jars . . ! In the associated village, and around its tank, preparations were being made for the Navarathri festival to the local gods which involved the contruction of vast structures (some on wheels). It was unclear (as our taxi driver couldn't tell us) what would happen to these structures - would they be set alight at the end of the festival and how on earth would the ones on wheels be moved?
