The festival also had something to do with the ritual of handing over the sword of the erstwhile Maharajas of Travancore at the palace and which many devotees would throng to the temple to witness. Clearly one of the "mysteries of the orient" ... . !

title: 12.Kanyakumari
text: Kerala & Tamil Nadu - 2004 Kanyakumari At the southernmost extremity of the Indian subcontinent, Kanyakumari is the meeting point of the Bay of Bengal, Indian Ocean and the Arabian Sea. It is a popular pilgrimage destination and is of great spiritual significance to Hindus, being dedicated to the goddess Devi Kanya, who is an incarnation of Devi, Shiva's wife. On shore, is the Kumari Amman Temple where she is worshipped - the image of her inside the temple wears a diamond nose stud of such brilliance it is said to be visible from the sea. Male visitors must be shirtless and wear a dhoti before entering the temple; non-Hindus are not allowed in the inner sanctum. Needless to say all these rules were waived for us upon payment of Rs 30 each ... n . ! O We took an overcrowded ferry from the jetty in Kanyakumari out to the Vivekananda Memorial which is on two rocky islands projecting from the sea about 400m offshore and which are known as the Pitru and Matru tirthas . In 1892 they attracted the attention of the hindu reformer Vivekananda (1862-1902) who swam out to the rocks to meditate. The Memorial build in 1970 houses a statue of the saint and the footprints of Kanya Devi can be seen here too - at the spot where she performed her penance. . ! We met some pilgrims - Hindu boys who were fasting, abstaining from meat, alcohol and sex. They were all very devout but clearly randy as hell.. . ! We then adjourned to the local beach where we watched the sun going down at the end of an eventful day. On full moon day (in April) it is said to be possible to watch the sun setting and the moon rising on the same horizon. We then returned to Trivandrum for a day of shopping - including our heavy statue of Vishnu - before catching our return flight home. . !

title: 1.Delhi
text: India - 2007 Delhi . After a long flight we arrived into Delhi, were met at the airport by the driver of our bed & breakfast home and then made our way into central Delhi where we found ourselves at Connaught Place . We took sanctuary in a branch of an 'Indian Coffee House' which we fondly remembered from our previous visit to Kerala in 2004. Up very early the next morning, we visited the main flower market where all sorts of flowers, plants and strings of marigolds were being bartered, sold and haggled over. It was bitterly cold as you can see from the fact that everyone appears to be wrapped up in scarves. After a quick stop for some deep-fried pakora for breakfast, we walked around the central area of Delhi and marvelled at some of the architectural styles on display. Visiting the main laundry district we saw whole families whose livelihoods depended on washing the clothes and sheets of the well-heeled inhabitants of up-market Delhi. West of Connaught Place, with soaring domes, the large Orissan-style Lakshmi Narayan Temple was erected in 1938 by the rich industrialist BD Birla. The main temple, inaugurated by Mahatma Gandhi, is dedicated to Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth. Delhi's main railway station was being rebuilt so it was complete chaos in that area. We did get a glimpse of the parcel delivery depot which was a hive of activity. We enjoyed the matching plant pots adorning the Sulabh Toilet Complex which is, in fact, a toilet museum ...

title: 2.Delhi Jantar Mantar
text: India - 2007 Delhi - Jantar Mantar . The Just a short stroll from Connaught Place is Jantar Mantar , the collection of salmon-coloured structures which were one of Maharaja Jai Singh II's amazing observatories (there is another one in Jaipur - see later ). Constructed in 1725 it is dominated by a huge sundial known as Samrat Yantra , the 'Prince of Dials'. Apart from the Samrat Yantra (a large sundial for calculating time), there is also Jai Prakash Yantra (2 concave hemispherical structures, used to ascertain the position of Sun and other heavenly bodies), Ram Yantra (two large cylindrical structures with open top, used to measure the altitude of stars based on the latitude and the longitude on the earth) and the Mishra Yantra (meaning mixed instrument, since it is a compilation of five different instruments). Honeymoon photos for one young couple on holiday.

title: 3.Delhi Red Fort
text: India - 2007 Delhi - Red Fort . The sandstone walls of the Red Fort extend for 2km and vary in height from 18m on the river side to 33m on the city side. Shah Jahan began construction in 1638 and the building was completed in 1648. He never completely moved his capital from Agra to the new city of 'Shahjahanabad' in Delhi because he was deposed and imprisoned in Agra Fort by his son Aurangzeb. The Red Fort dates from the very peak of Mughal Power but the Mughal reign from Delhi was a short one: Aurangzeb was the first and last great Mughal emperor to rule from here. The Yamuna River used to flow right by the eastern edge of the fort, and once filled the 10m-deep moat. Security was on red-alert due to the tensions between India and Pakistan. We had to pass through barriers manned by armed guards - as they genuinely feared an attack by terrorists which would wreck the tourism industry.

title: 4.Delhi Jama Masjid
text: India - 2007 Delhi - Jama Masjid . This striking mosque - the Jama Masjid - is the largest in India and the final architectural extravagance of Shah Jahan. Begun in 1644 the mosque wasn't completed until 1658. The mosque has three gateways, four towers and two minarets standing 40m high and is constructed of alternating vertical strips of red sandstone and white marble. The area around the mosque was heaving with people, children playing football and stallholders selling merchandise. We particularly liked these big red bras for sale within striking distance of the conservative mosque ... Gracefully appointed, with pillared verandahs and an avenue of palms, the Imperial Hotel is an eclectic Raj-era hotel build in 1931, and has hosted everyone from royalty to rock stars. Indeed, it's said that Gandhi, Jinnah, Nehru and Mountbatten met here to discuss the thorny matter of India's partition. Beautifully refurbished, the property amalgamates various styles, from classic Victorian to colonial and Art Deco. It has two fabulous bars - at one of which we managed to sink £50 on four gins and tonics ...

title: 5.Amritsar
text: India - 2007 Amritsar - Golden Temple . Taking a nine-hour 'express' rail journey on the Shatabdi Express , we arrived into Amritsar almost on the border with Pakistan. Its most famous site is the fabled Golden Temple , spiritual centre of the Sikh faith. Built by Guru Arjan Dev in the late sixteenth century, the richly gilded Harmandir rises from the middle of a rectangular articial lake, connected to the white marble complex that surrounds it by a small causeway. Every devout member of the Sikh faith tries to make at least one pilgrimage here in their lifetime for darshan of the original Sikh holy book, the Adi Granth , and to bathe in the purifying waters of the temple tank. The large dome on its gilded roof, decked with 100kg of gold leaf, is in the form of an inverted lotus, symbolising the Sikhs' concern for temporal as well as spiritual matters. The Golden Temple is also renowned for two bloody battles waged in the 1980s when the Akal Takht (the second most sacred shrine in the complex) was occupied by Sikh militants. The siege was brought to an end in June 1984 when prime minister Indira Ghandi ordered a paramilitary attack on the temple, code-named 'Operation Blue Star'. An estimated 200 soldiers and 2,000 others (including pilgrims trapped in the gurudwaras ) were killed. Widely regarded as an unmitigated disaster, 'Blue Star' led directly to the assassination of Indira Ghandi by her Sikh bodyguards just four months later, and provoked the worst riots in the city since Partition . Visitors of all nationalities and religions are allowed into the Golden Temple provided they follow a few basic rules which are enforced by patrolling guards (see photo below). Alcohol, tobacco and drugs of any kind are forbidden and shoes must be left in the cloakrooms and your head covered by some kind of cloth.

title: 6.Amritsar
text: India - 2007 Amritsar - Hotel . We stayed in the delightful Svaasa Hotel - a smart refurbishment of a 200 year old British Colonial Haveli, now plush with its characteristic boutique rooms and suites, fully equipped with modern amenities. The open courtyard has landscaped greenery and the rooftop has vegetation too. The Mehras, the Royal family descendants who personally manage and run this place, make it a rich experience.

title: 7.Amritsar
text: India - 2007 Amritsar - Adi Granth . The triple-storeyed Harmandir , the 'Golden Temple of God' from which the complex takes its name, was built by Arjan Dev to house the Adi Granth , or 'Original Book', which he compiled from the teachings of all the Sikh gurus, and which still forms the lynchpin of the Sikh faith. Instead of the usual single door, the temple has four to indicate that it is open to people of all faiths and to all four caste divisions of Hindu society . The long causeway, or Guru's Bridge, which joins the mandir to the west side of the Amrit Sarovar , is approached via an ornate archway, the Darshani Deorhi , where worshippers collect dollops of sticky sweet porridge on a leaf, prasad that will later be placed as an offering in the shrine itself. The interior of the temple, dripping in yet more gold and silver, and adorned with ivory mosaics and intricately-carved wood panels, is dominated by the enormous Adi Granth , which rests on a sumptuous throne beneath a jewel-encrusted silk canopy. Before his death in 1708, Guru Gobind Singh, who revised the Adi Granth , declared that he was to be the last living Guru and the Holy Book would take over as Guru after him. Accordingly the Book is given 'human' status and is recited from in continuous readings which are carried out in three-hour shifts and take a total of 48 hours to complete. At the end of the day, the Adi Granth is paraded around the Harmandir and then put to bed, literally wrapped up in blankets for the night. When we were there, the blankets were made from artificial fibres and featured images of Winnie the Pooh ... Our taxi back to the hotel.

title: 8.Amritsar
text: India - 2007 Amritsar - Jallianwala Bagh . 100m north-east of the Golden Temple is a narrow lane which leads between two tall buildings to Jallianwala Bagh - site of one of the bloodiest atrocities committed in the history of the British Raj. In 1919, a series of one-day strikes was staged in Amritsar in protest against the Rowlatt Act which enabled the British to imprison, without trial, any Indian suspected of sedition. Martial Law was declared and a platoon of infantry arrived, led by General REH Dyer. Despite a ban on public meetings, a demonstration was called by Mahatma Ghandi for 13 April, the Sikh holiday of Bhaisakhi . An estimated 20,000 people gathered at Jallianwala Bagh for the meeting but, before any speakers could address the throng, Dyer and his 150 troops blocked the exit and fired on the crowd. Many people died (official estimates put the death toll at 372, with 1,200 injured) although the final figure may well have been three to four times this amount. Many people died by throwing themselves down the well in the middle of the Bagh in order to avoid the bullets. Hushed up for over six months in the UK, the massacre caused an international outcry when the story finally broke and it proved seminal in the Independence struggle, prompting Ghandi to initiate the widespread civil disobedience campaign that played such a significant part in ridding India of its colonial overlords . Then into the old town centre to people-watch and browse in shops. We found this charming potato crisp seller with his son and friend. The crisps were flavourless but we felt obliged to buy some ...

title: 9.Amritsar
text: India - 2007 Amritsar - Durgiana Mandir . The Durgiana Mandir , though a Hindu temple, has architecture very similar to the Golden Temple. This temple derives its name from the Goddess Durga. Idols of Goddess Lakshmi (Goddess of Wealth) and Vishnu (Protector of the World) are also deified and worshipped. It was built in 1921 by Guru Harsai Mal Kapoor, in the middle of a sacred lake. Its dome and canopies are similar to that of the Golden Temple and also has a bridge to provide the approach to the main building. The dome is illuminated with colourful lights. It is sometimes called the Silver Temple because of its large exquisitely designed silver doors. It has a rich collection of Hindu scriptures. Here, children act out the roles of Goddess Durga and her consorts - although the story was far from clear ... Tableaux of Lakshmi and Vishnu are blessed by the priest while other vignettes are staged behind glass.

title: 10.Agra
text: India - 2007 Agra - Taj Mahal . Described as the most extravagant monument ever built for love, this sublime Mughal mausoleum is India's tourist emblem. Many have tried to sum up its beauty - ' a teardrop on the face of eternity ' according to Indian poet Rabindranath Tagore, ' the embodiment of all things pure ' according to Rudyard Kipling. As an architectural masterpiece, the Taj Mahal stands head and shoulders above any other contender. The Taj was built by Emperor Shah Jahan as a memorial for his second wife, Mumtaz Mahal, who died giving birth to their fourteenth child in 1631. The death of Mumtaz left the Emperor so heartbroken that his hair turned white overnight. Construction of the Taj began the same year but was not completed until 1653. In total 20,000 people from India and Central Asia worked on the building. Specialists were brought in from as far afield as Europe to produce the exquisite marble screens and pietra dura (marble inlay work) made with thousands of semi-precious stones. But first, we had to get into the monument. Tight security was in place and Seán looks pretty cheesed off and had to hand over his cigarettes and lighter. The construction bill for the Taj Mahal is believed to have run to Rs 3 million, equivalent to about US$70 million today. As well as the architecture, we enjoyed watching other visitors . Having been on site all day, we were able to see the light changing in the sky and on the building. The white marble appeared to change colour from brilliant white in the morning, to a pale yellow in the early evening and finally a pale pink before the sun set. Beautiful.

title: 11.Agra
text: India - 2007 Agra - Akbar's Tomb . This outstanding mausoleum commemorates the greatest of the Mughal emperors. The huge courtyard is entered through a stunning gateway. It has three-storey minarets at each corner and is built of red sandstone strikingly inlaid with white marble geometric patterns. The tomb itself lies in the centre of a peaceful garden, where deer graze, monkeys play in the trees and raucous peacocks and parakeets make their presence felt. Akbar's cenotaph is in the mausoleum but the true tomb, as per traditions, lies below it. After his death, Akbar's son Jahangir completed the construction in 1605–1613. During the reign of Aurangzeb, Jats rose in rebellion under the leadership of Raja Ram Jat. Mughal prestige suffered a blow when Jats ransacked Akbar's tomb, plundering and looting the gold, jewels, silver and carpets. According to one account, even Akbar's grave was opened and his bones burned.

title: 12.Agra
text: India - 2007 Agra - Itimad-ud-Daulah . Nicknamed the Baby Taj, the Itimad-ud-Daulah is the exquisite tomb of Mizra Ghiyas Beg and was the first Mughal structure totally built from marble and the first to make extensive use of pietra dura . Mizra Ghiyas Beg was a Persian nobleman who was Jehangir's wazir (chief minister). His daughter, Nur Jahan, who married Jehangir, built the tomb between 1622 and 1628 in a style similar to the tomb she built for Jehangir near Lahore in Pakistan. Then we visited the Chini-ka-Rauza , a Persian-style riverside tomb of Afzal Khan, a poet and high official in the court of Shah Jahan. It was built between 1628 and 1639. This relatively unknown mausoleum is hidden away down a shady avenue of trees. Bright blue tiles still cover part of the exterior and the interior is painted in floral designs. As we were on the other side of the Yamuna River, it gave us the opportunity to view the Taj Mahal from behind which was unusual, seeing it from fields planted by farmers, as it has looked for nigh on 500 years.

title: 13.Agra Fort
text: India - 2007 Agra Fort . Construction of the massive red sandstone Agra Fort on the bank of the Yamuna River, was begun by Emperior Akbar in 1565. Further additions were made, particularly by his grandson Shah Jahan, who added buildings using his favourite white marble. The fort was built primarily as a military structure, but Shah Jahan upgraded it to a palace, and later it became his gilded prison for eight years after his son, Aurangzeb, seized power in 1658. The Zanjir-i-Adl is where Mughal king Jahangir (born Prince Salim) instituted his 'chain of justice' in c.1605. He records in his memoir that after his accession, the first order he gave, " was for the fastening up of the chain of justice so that if those engaged in the administration of justice should delay or practice hypocrisy, the aggrieved might come to this chain and shake it so that its noise might attract my attention. " It was made of pure gold, 80 foot in length and had 60 bells. One end was fastened to the battlements of the Shah-Burj and the other end to a stone post on the bank of the river. It was a way to redress the grievances of the people who could approach the king, the highest judicial authority of the empire, directly, without fee, fear or formality for immediate relief and with no distinction of caste or creed or between poor and rich. Jahangir's administration of justice became a legend in Indian history. The Diwan-i-Am (Hall of Public Audiences) was used by Shah Jahan for domestic government business and features a throne room where the emperor listened to petitioners. By contrast, the Diwan-i-Khas (Hall of Private Audiences) was reserved for important dignitaries or foreign representives. The Khas Mahal is the palace where Shah Jahan was imprisoned for eight years and from where he could look out at the Taj Mahal where his wife was buried. The Musamman Burj is a wonderful white marble octagonal tower which was part of the Khas Mahal in which Shah Jahan was imprisoned. Overlooking the river and the distant Taj Mahal is Takhti-i-Jahangir , a huge slab of black rock with an inscription around the edge. This throne was made for Jahangir when he was Prince Salim. In the courtyard of the large harem quarters is Anguri Bagh , a graden that has been brought back to life and now looks like it may have done in Shah Jahan's time.

title: 14.Agra
text: India - 2007 Agra Haircut & Drink . Seán was looking a bit shaggy and needed a haircut. We found an obliging barber in the back streets of Agra who duly washed and cut Seán's hair. An old school friend of Philip (Peter Foster) was a hotel manager in the expensive Oberoi chain. He had previously been based in Bali but had recently moved to Dubai. However, he was able to arrange for us to have some free drinks at the Agra Oberoi. And very nice it was too.

title: 15.Fatehpur Sikri
text: India - 2007 Fatehpur Sikri . This magnificent fortified ghost city was the Mughal empire's short-lived capital between 1571 and 1585, during the reign of Akbar. Although brilliant from an architectural point of view, Akbar's city was built in an area that suffered from water shortages and it was abandoned shortly after his death. Entrance is through the enormous Buland Darwaza (Victory Gate), perhaps the largest in Asia, built to commemorate Akbar's military victory in Gujarat. The beautiful Jama Masjid (Dargah Mosque) completed in 1571, contains elements of both Persian and Hindu design. Inside the courtyard is the superb white marble Tomb of Shaikh Salim Chishti , completed in 1581. Inside the mausoleum are brightly-coloured flower murals and the canopy is decorated with mother-of-pearl shell. Just as Akbar came to the saint four centuries before hoping for a son, childless women visit his tomb today and tie a thread to the jalis (marble lattice screens) which are among the finest in India. A Quranic inscription inside the archway quotes Jesus saying - ' The world is a bridge, pass over it but build no house upon it. He who hopes for an hour may hope for eternity ', which seems appropriate considering the fate of the city. The lack of water can be seen in the depth in the Ornamental Pool . The whimsical Panch Mahal is a five storey pavilion that was used by the court ladies. Each of the storeys is reduced in size until the top one consists of only a tiny kiosk. The lower floor has 84 columns, all of which are different. The so-called Astrologer's Kiosk has its roof supports carved into a serpentine Jain style. The Diwan-i-Khas (Hall of Private Audience) has an interior which is dominated by a magnificently carved stone column in the centre. The pillar flares to create a flat-topped plinth linked to the four corners of the room by narrow stone bridges, from where Akbar is believed to have debated with scholars who stood at the ends of the four bridges. We watched some daredevil kids tombstoning into the filthy water of the Tank . The Hiran Minar (Elephant Tower), is a bizarre circular tower covered with stone projections in the form of elephant tusks. Traditionally it was thought to have been erected as a memorial to the Emperor Akbar's favourite elephant. However, it was probably used as a starting point for subsequent mileposts. We walked back into the town where we enjoyed a delicious rooftop thali supper before we retired to the Gulistan Tourist Complex for the night.

title: 16.Balaji
text: India - 2007 Balaji . Mehandipur Balaji Mandir is an extraordinary exorcism temple, dedicated to the Hindu God Hanuman. The name Balaji is applied to Shri Hanuman in several parts of India because the childhood ( Bala in Hindi / Sanskrit) form of the Lord is especially celebrated there. People bring their loved ones who are suffering from possession to have bad spirits exorcised through prayer and rituals. At this time, the only people who can enter the temple are the holy men and the victims - services are relayed to the crowds outside on crackly video screens. Below are two Mehandipur Balaji idols from the temple. 'Dussehra' celebrates the Hindu god Rama's victory over Ravana and the triumph of good over evil. The epic Ramayana tells the story of Lord Rama who wins the lovely Sita for his wife, only to have her carried off by Ravana, the demon king of Lanka. An effigy of Ravana is burned which marks 'Dussehra', burning of evil and spreading of light marking 'Diwali'. Believers say you should not take items bought from around the temple away with you since they could bring you bad luck. But the number of stalls lining the way to the temple indicates that not everyone heeds these solemn warnings. Outside Balaji we passed vast brick works with odd conical-shaped chimneys. Not quite the dark Satanic mills of lore, they still appeared strange in this arid landscape.

title: 17.Abhaneri
text: India - 2007 Abhaneri . This remote village is an unlikely location for one of Rajasthan's most awe-inspiring wells, the Chand Baori. With around 11 visible levels of zigzagging steps, this 10th century water tank is an incredible geometric sight, 20m deep. Flanking the baori is a small, crumbling palace where the royals used to bathe in private rooms - it's now inhabited by pigeons and bats. It is thought to have been built by King Chand, ruler of Abhaneri and a Rajput from the Chahmana dynasty.

title: 18.Galtaji
text: India - 2007 Galtaji . Galtaji is an ancient Hindu pilgrimage about 10km away from Jaipur. The site consists of a series of temples built into a narrow pass in the Aravalli Hills. A natural spring emerges high on the hills and flows downward, filling a series of sacred kunds (water tanks) in which pilgrims bathe. Visitors and pilgrims can ascend the crevasse, continuing past the highest water pool to a hilltop temple from there are views of Jaipur spread out across the valley floor. It is believed that a saint named Galav lived here, practiced meditation and did tapasya (penance). The Sita Ram Ji Temple Complex is colloquially known as the Monkey Temple ( Galwar Bagh ) in travel literature, due to the large number of rhesus macaque monkeys which live in the largely abandoned and only partially-restored temples.

title: 19.Amber Fort
text: India - 2007 Amber Fort . The delicate, magnificent, pink fort-palace of Amber , an ethereal example of Rajput architecture, rises from a rocky mountinside about 11km north-east of Jaipur. Amber was the ancient capital of Jaipur state. Maota Lake, which dries out during the hot season, and Kesar Kyari (Saffron Garden). A narrow and very steep road leads up to the entrance gate, known as the Suraj Pol (Sun Gate) of the fort. We walked up as we refused to take an elephant ride: we did not wish to partake in the mistreatment of these noble beasts since there is significant evidence of inhumane practices with their care. An imposing staircase leads up to the main palace but first we went into the small Kali Temple which has beautiful silver doors featuring repoussé (raised relief) work. Above the lintel to the temple is an image of Ganesh, this one carved from a single piece of coral. Then we arrived into the Diwan-i-Am (Hall of Public Audience) which has a double row of columns, each topped by a capital in the shape of an elephant, and latticed galleries above. Here the maharaja held audience and received the petitions of his subjects. The maharaja's apartments are entered through the fabulous Ganesh Pol , decorated with mosaics and sculptures. It is a three-level structure with many frescoes that was built at the orders of the Mirza Raja Jai Singh (1621–1627). Above this gate is the Suhag Mandir where ladies of the royal family used to watch functions held in the Diwan-i-Am through latticed marble windows ( jalis ). The Jai Mandir (Hall of Victory) is noted for its inlaid panels and multi-mirrored ceiling. Patterns made with coloured foil and paint are covered in glass. At night this would have been candle-lit and the convex mirrors would have glittered brightly. It is also known as Sheesh Mahal (Mirror Palace) but, however, most of the mirror work was allowed to deteriorate but is now in the process of restoration and renovation. Opposite the Jai Mandir is the Sukh Niwas (Hall of Pleasure) which has a water channel running through the room which acted as an ingenious air-cooling system. Not a single drop of water was wasted, with the overflow passing through conduits to the gardens. The garden was built by Mirza Raja Jai Singh (1623–68) and is patterned on the lines of the Chahar Bagh (Mughal Garden). I n a sunken bed and laid out with narrow channels lined with marble around a star-shaped pool with a fountain at the centre. Water for the garden flows in cascades through channels from the Sukh Niwas and also from the channels called the chini khana that originate on the terrace of the Jai Mandir. Further examples of jalis (latticed mable windows). The Suhag Mandir where ladies of the royal family used to look down on functions held in the Diwan-i-Am through latticed marble screens ( jalis ). The Diwan-i-Khas (Hall of Private Audiences) was reserved for important dignitaries or foreign representives.

title: 20.Jaipur
text: India - 2007 Jaipur . Jaipur (known as the Pink City) was founded in 1727 by the Rajput ruler Jai Singh II, the ruler of Amer (Amber), after whom the city is named. It was one of the earliest planned cities of modern India, designed by Vidyadhar Bhattacharya. During the British Colonial period, the city served as the capital of Jaipur State. After independence in 1947, Jaipur was made capital of the newly-formed state of Rajasthan. The Hawa Mahal (The Palace of Winds) is a structure built in 1799 by Maharaja Sawai Pratap Singh, the grandson of Jai Singh II, the founder of Jaipur. Designed by Lal Chand Ustad, its unique five floors exterior is akin to the honeycomb of a beehive with its 953 small windows called Jharokhas decorated with intricate latticework which allows the breeze to pass through. The original intent of the lattice design was to allow royal ladies to observe everyday life and festivals celebrated in the street below without being seen, since they had to obey the strict rules of 'purdah'. Walking around the market square, the Badi Chaupar , and the Tripolia Bazaar we saw a vast range of items for sale, from star fruit, to tubas, to peanuts and stockings. A visit to the Sanganer Paper Factory where we saw brightly coloured pages being produced from raw dyed pulp. Many of the sheets have rose petals incorporated in them. We also met the owner, a rather grumpy man but with a delightful daughter who made us feel very welcome. The Albert Hall , built in honour of the Prince of Wales' 1876 visit, now houses the Central Museum. It was designed by Sir Swinton Jacob and combines elements of English and North Indian architecture. The gardens were in part a famine-relief project to provide work for the unemployed. On the day we visited, the museum appeared to have as many pigeons inside as visitors. The Raj Mandir cinema was an unusual 1950s-style building to be found in the middle of an Indian city. Our accommodation, the Hotel Meghniwas , was in a building erected by Brigadier Singh in 1950 and now run by his gracious decendants. It also had a refreshing swimming pool. That evening on our way back from supper, we passed an amazing wedding party with the bridegroom on horseback with his nephew. We were invited to attend the wedding banquet but declined as we had already eaten.

title: 21.Jaipur Jantar Mantar
text: India - 2007 Jaipur - Jantar Mantar . Jaipur also has a Jantar Mantar , the name of which is derived from the Sanskrit yanta mantr (meaning 'instrument of calculation'). It was begun by Jai Singh in 1728 who was keen to measure time by the sun falling on huge sundials and charting its annual progress through the zodiac. Jai Singh liked astronomy even more than he liked war and town planning. Before constructing the observatory, he sent scholars abroad to study foreign constructs. Jai Singh built five observatories in total: this is the largest and best preserved (it was restored in 1901). Others are in Delhi , Varanasi and Ujjain. The fifth, the Mathura observatory, has disappeared.

title: 22.Pushkar
text: India - 2007 Pushkar . Pushkar is a Hindu pilgrimage town which curls around a holy lake, said to have appeared when Brahma dropped a lotus flower. Besides pilgrims, travellers have also discovered Pushkar's charms and small, whitewashed budget guesthouses almost outnumber the temples. The result is a muddle of religion, commerce and a lot of wasted westerners who appear to have been here since the 1960s having found the bhang cheap and plentiful. A cluster of pale onion-shaped domes surround the lake. These are temples where regular pujas create the town's soundtrack of chanting, drums and gongs and devotional songs booming out from crackling speakers. Few of the temples in Pushkar are ancient as they were mostly desecrated by Aurangzeb (son of Shah Jahan) and have subsequently been rebuilt. Most famous is the Brahma Temple which is marked by a red spire. Inside the floor and wall are engraved with dedications to the dead. Many of the priests seemed charming until you refused to give them money in exchange for a puja (prayer) and a red ribbon or a flower, when they turned unpleasantly aggressive. Around the lake are fifty-two bathing ghats where pilgrims bathe in the sacred water. Some ghats have particular importance: Vishnu appeared at Varah Ghat in the form of a boar, Brahma bathed at Brahma Ghat and Gandhi's ashes were sprinkled at Gandhi Ghat (formerly Gau Ghat). Our accommodation at the Hotel Everest did not appear particularly appealing, but it did have fabulous rooftop views of surrounding buildings and the hills beyond. This is the hotel where we should have stayed - the Seventh Heaven - but, due to an administrative error by the owner, he had booked us in June 2007 rather than January 2007 ... However, we went there for supper one night and found it delightful. Our hotel did however give us fantastic views at sunrise and sunset.

title: 23.Chittorgarh
text: India - 2007 Chittorgarh . Chittorgarh has one of the most splendid and impressive forts in all of Rajasthan. It is mentioned in the Mahabharata when Bhim (one of the Pandava heroes) struck the ground so hard that water gushed out to form a large reservoir. The fort, dating from the 8th century, was built around that reservoir. The fort stands on a 28 sq km site on top of a hill that rises abruptly from the surrounding plain. Until 1568 the town of Chittor was within the fort walls, but today's modern town (known as Lower Town) sprawls to the west of the hill. We entered the fort by the Suraj Pol from which we enjoyed fantastic views across the plains. l. We e The Jaya Stambha (Tower of Victory) was erected by Rana Kumbha between 1458 and 1468 to commemorate his victory over Mahmud Khilji of Malwa in 1440. It rises 37m in nine exquisitely carved storeys. The intensely carved Sammidheshwar Temple , built in the 6th century and restored in 1427, is nearby. There is also space for a Jain Temple. This is called Neelkanth Mahadev . Walk down beyond the temples and, at the edge of the cliff, is a deep tank - the Gaumukh Reservoir - where you can feed the fish. The reservoir takes its name from a spring that feeds the tank from a cow's mouth carved into the hillside. The Singa Chowri Temple , built in 1448, has amazing and intricate carving around its exterior. The Kirti Stambha (Tower of Fame) is smaller than the Tower of Victory, only standing 22m high. Built by a Jain merchant, the tower is dedicated to Adinath and is decorated with naked figures of the various tirthankars (Jain teachers). The ruins of the 15th century Rana Kumbha Palace include elephant and horse stables and a Shiva Temple. The Meera Temple was built in the reign of Rana Kumbha (1433-1468) in the ornate Indo-Aryan style and associated with with the mystic poetess Meerabai.

title: 24.Castle Bijaipur
text: India - 2007 Castle Bijaipur . The 350-year old Castle Bijaipur is set amidst the Vindhyanchal hills and is now run as a heritage hotel by the ruling family. In a brilliant location, we were given a drum fanfare as we arrived. We showered, relaxed and enjoyed supper under the stars where we were entertained by local musicians and a dancer.

title: 25.Udaipur
text: India - 2007 Udaipur . Our accommodation in Udaipur was the scenic Amet Haveli , another 350-year old building which this time was on the lakeshore overlooking Udaipur City Palace and the luxurious Lake Palace Hotel. We enjoyed a late lunch while bathers dived off Hanuman Ghat . It was a wonderful location and it felt more Mediterranean than Indian, that is until the bathers started hawking and clearing out their nasal passages ... Later, from the City Palace, it was possible to look back over our accommodation ( Amet Haveli ), the low white building in the centre of the photo below. After our lunch we crossed the bridge at the head of the lake and wandered around the old town. Seán made friends with a tame bullock and calf. In a cafe where we stopped for a drink we were not unduly shocked by the filth of the toilet (we were used to this by now) but were astonished by the branding on it ... We ended up in the atmospheric Savage Garden for a beer and supper and from where we enjoyed fabulous views of the sunset over Udaipur Lake.

title: 26.Udaipur Ahar
text: India - 2007 Udaipur - Ahar . About 2km east of Udaipur, at Ahar , are more than 250 restored cenotaphs of the maharajas of Mewar, forming a spectacular, if ghostly, city of snowy domes built over 350 years. About 19 former maharajas were cremated here. The peace and tranquillity of this remote spot was shattered when what sounded like a Mariachi band started up. It was the local trumpet and drum band practising for a forthcoming parade ... The most striking cenotaph is that of Maharaja Amar Singh, who ruled from 1597 to 1620. One of the cenotaphs was cracked and it was alarming to be able to see right down into the tomb ...

title: 27.Udaipur Moti Magri
text: India - 2007 Udaipur - Moti Magri . Overlooking Fateh Sagar lake (north of Udaipur) atop Moti Magri (Pear Hill), is a statue of the Rajput hero Maharana Pratap, who frequntly defied the Mughals while riding his beloved-horse, Chetak. The path to the top of the hill traverses some pleasant gardens. The bloody Siege of Chittorgarh in 1568 had led to the loss of the fertile eastern belt of Mewar to the Mughals. However, the rest of the kingdom was still under the control of the Rana. The Mughal emperor Akbar was intent on securing a stable route to Gujarat through Mewar. When Pratap Singh was crowned king (Rana) in 1572, Akbar sent a number of envoys entreating the Rana to become a vassal like many other Rajput leaders in the region. When the Rana refused to submit to Akbar, war became inevitable. The Battle of Haldighati was fought on 18 June 1576 between Maharana Pratap and Akbar's forces led by Man Singh I of Amer. After a fierce battle lasting more than six hours, Maharana found himself wounded and the day lost but the Mughals were unable to capture him. He managed to escape to the hills and lived to fight another day. Haldighati was a futile victory for the Mughals, since they were unable to capture Maharana Pratap, or any of his close family members in Udaipur. As soon as the empire's focus shifted north-west, Pratap and his army came out of hiding and recaptured the western regions of his dominion. The maharajas' Vintage & Classic Car Collection is fascinating. Housed in the former state garage are 22 splendid vehicles, including a 1938 Cadillac complete with purdah system, a beautiful 1934 Rolls Royce used in Octopussy , a homely little Morris Minor Traveller from 1959, the Cadillac convertible that whisked Queen Elizabeth II to the airport in 1961 and even a horse-drawn carriage.

title: 28.Udaipur City Palace
text: India - 2007 Udaipur - City Palace . The imposing City Palace is Rajasthan's largest palace with a façade 244m long and 30m high. Surmounted by balconies, towers, cupolas and extended and altered by various maharajas, it still manages to retain a surprising uniformity of design . Construction was begun by Maharaja Udai Singh II, the city's founder, in 1553 when he moved the capital from Chittorgarh to Udaipur. The rooms of the Museum are extravagantly decorated with mirrors, glass, tiles and mirrors. In the Manak Mahal (Ruby Palace) there is exquisite coloured glass work. The Sheesh Mahal features extraordinary mirrors and seems to have been the inspiration for many 1970s discotheques. There is a wonderful coolness and air of sophistication in the Zenana Mahal (Ladies Chamber) which is now apparently used as a venue for weddings. This opens onto Laxmi Chowk with a pretty pavilion in the middle of the square. There is also a large tiger cage which worked like a giant mousetrap. A goat or bullock would be tied up inside as a tiger-tempting snack, and tiger would be lured into captivity. The Surya Chopar has a huge ornamental sun, the symbol of the sun-descended Mewar dynasty. The private rooms of Rajmata Gulabkunwar (The Queen's Room). Many palaces in India have a Durbar Hall (Royal Court). Usually the grandest room in the palace it was used by India's rulers for official occasions, such as state banquets, and to hold meetings. The restored Durbar Hall in Udaipur is one of the most impressive (with some of the biggest chandeliers you've ever seen). The foundation stone was laid in 1909 by Lord Minto (Viceroy of India) during the reign of Maharaja Fateh Singh. The top floor is surrounded by viewing galleries where ladies of the court could watch what was happening below. Incorporated in the Palace is the Government Museum which houses some wonderful pieces of 5th century sculpture, a cabinet of Maharaja's heads documenting the changing fashions of the moustache, a freaky monkey holding a lamp, the chain mail of Rajput hero Maharana Pratap and a horse with a contraption which disguised it as an elephant.

title: 29.Udaipur Pichola Lake
text: India - 2007 Udaipur - Pichola Lake . Limpid and large, Pichola Lake spreads from the shores of the city, reflecting the cool grey mountains on its rippling surface. It was enlarged by Udai Singh II after he founded the city. He flooded Picholi village, which gave its name to the lake. The lake is now 4km long and 3km wide, but it remains shallow and dries up in severe droughts when it is possible to walk to Jagniwas and Jagmandir , the two major islands on the lake . The Lake Palace Hotel is on the island of Jagniwas was built by Maharaja Jagat Singh II in 1754. Once the royal summer palace, it was converted into a hotel in the 1960s by Maharaja Bhagwat Singh and was greatly extended. It is the ultimate in luxury hotels and was largely responsible for putting Udaipur on the international tourist map. We took a tour boat across the lake, passing the Lake Palace Hotel and landing on the island of Jagmandir where we viewed the palace built by Maharaja Karan Singh in 1620. It is said that Shah Jahan (then Prince Kharrim) derived some of his inspiration for the Taj Mahal after staying here in 1623. It's a pretty island with a row of enormous stone elephants facing the lake and neat courtyards with fragrant frangipani trees. Back on our tour boat from which we could see the City Palace and Lake Palace Hotel glowing golden in the evening sun. We also saw another spectacular sunset.

title: 30.Udaipur Jagdish Temple
text: India - 2007 Udaipur - Jagdish Temple . 150m north of the City Palace is the fantastically carved Indo-Aryan Jagdish Temple which was built by Maharaja Jagat Singh in 1651. It enshrines a black stone image of Vishnu as Jagannath, Lord of the Universe. The temple steps are flanked by stone elephants and there is intricate and ornate carving around all the plinths and outside the temple walls. Seán got a dose of the 'Delhi belly' and had to remain in bed while I went to The Spice Box for a lesson in curry making. The teacher was a very patient and gentle chap and I enjoyed the food I had cooked at the end of the lesson.

title: 31.Ranakpur
text: India - 2007 Ranakpur . On the road between Udaipur and Jodhpur, Ranakpur is one of India's biggest and most important Jain temples. The main temple is called the Chaumukha Mandir (Four-Faced Temple) dedicated to Adinath and built in 1439. The building is constructed from milk-white marble and is an astonishingly complicated series of 29 halls supported by a forest of 1,444 pillars, no two of which are alike. The interior is completely covered in intricate carving. The devotion of its builders is shown in the complex architecture and loving carving, and the pale interior has an unparalled sense of space and harmony. This is the main shrine of the Jain Temple. The deity of Parshwanath with 1,008 heads of snakes and numerous tails. Depiction of Jambudvipa . Adjacent to the Jain Temple is the Sun Temple built about 100 years before the Jain Temple. It features some erotic carvings. We had a problem with one of the wheels of the car and had to stop for repairs. Everyone had a view on what to do, but it was sorted within an hour and we could continue on our drive to Jodhpur.

title: 32.Jodhpur
text: India - 2007 Jodhpur . The desert city of Jodhpur is dominated by the huge Meherangarh Fort (above in the background behind the Jaswant Thada Cenotaph ). Described as the 'Blue City' it really is blue, painted as if to reflect the colour of a hot sky. As well as glowing with a mysterious light, the colour is thought to repel insects. Jodhpur was founded by Rao Jodha and is on the vital trade route between Delhi and Gujarat. It grew out of the profits of opium, sandalwood, dates and copper and the area was once cheerily known as Marwar (the 'Land of Death') due to its harsh topography and climate. Jodhpur is a very hectic place cluttered with traffic but, to be honest, feels poorer and less developed than the cities of the east. The Clock Tower is an old city landmark, surrounded by the vibrant Sardar Market . At our accommodation - Pal Haveli , which was built around a courtyard by the Thakur of Pal in 1847 - it was time to say goodbye to our driver, Anit, who had driven us faithfully from Delhi all the way to Jodhpur. The view from the roof terrace was spectacular, overlooking the Clock Tower in one direction and the Meherangarh Fort the other, which we saw as the sun set and the moon and stars came out.

title: 33.Meherangarh
text: India - 2007 Jodhpur - Meherangarh Fort . Following the lines of a 125m hill, the fort's height becomes apparent as you approach it. The battlements are up to 36m high and, as the bulding materials were chiselled from the rock on which the fort stands, the structure seems to merge and grow from its base. The fort is still owned and run by the current Maharaja of Jodhpur but has been added to over the centuries by the reigning Maharajas. The fort has seven pols (gates). The view back over Jodhpur is really stunning and you can see from this height why the town has the name of the 'Blue City'. The Lohapol (Iron Gate) is built after a sharp turn to stop onslaughts by an enemy's elephants. It also has iron spikes as a further elephant deterrent. Beside the gate are tiny handprints, the sati (self-immolation) marks of Maharaja Man Singh's widows who threw themselves on his funeral pyre in 1843 - the last sati widows of the Jodhpur dynasty. The handprints still attract devotional attention. Inside the fort is a terracotta-latticed network of courtyards and palaces. Through the gate is Singhar Chowk , where coronations took place. The small marble seat was used for coronations from the 17th century onwards. The museum holds a splendid collection of Indian royal trappings, including elephant howdahs , some of which feature repoussé silverwork. There are also palanquins including covered ones for women in purdah. The finest one is that presented to Jaswant Singh I by the Emperor Shah Jahan; it's exquisitely worked in silver and gold and features a built-in umbrella to beat the heat. The museum also displays some devotional idols and some fabulous miniatures including the one below of Maharaja Gaj Singh I (1595-1638). Within the complex are numerous small chambers with evocative names such as the Sheesh Mahal (Hall of Mirrors). On the floor above is the Phool Mahal (Flower Palace) in which traditional dances were performed. The fine paintings adorning the walls of this palace were executed by a single artist who took 10 years to create them using a curious concoction of gold leaf, glue and cow's urine. The fort enjoys fantastic views, both internally and out over the city of Jodhpur. The private chamber of Maharaja Thakhat Singh (1843-1873) is called Thakhat Vilas . He had no less than 30 Maharanis and numerous concubines. The beautiful ceiling is adorned with glass Christmas baubles. In the zenana (women's apartments), the Jhanki Mahal has cradles of infant princes including that of the current Maharaja - a motorised version. The early-17th century Moti Mahal (Pearl Palace) is where the royal women would hold meetings. The walls are coated with seashell dust and the five alcoves along the western wall were for oil lamps. The gold-painted ceiling is embellished with glass tiles. We were not quite sure whether a real wedding was taking place here or if these people were actors pretending to be a Maharaja and his wife and/or concubine. The costumes were all splendid but were let down by the following woman holding a plastic bottle of water ...

title: 34.Ahmedabad Diu
text: India - 2007 Ahmedabad and Diu . From Jodhpur we took a train to Ahmedabad where we stayed in one of the cheap but grim 'railway retirement rooms'. Still, they had clean sheets even if the walls were filthy and there were cockroaches in the bathroom. From there we took a bus to Bhavnagar where we hired a taxi which took us on the final section of our journey to Diu . It was a relief to arrive at the Radhika Resort for some relative comfort and a clean environment - even if they did have tacky neon lights and illuminated Grecian goddesses. The little island of Diu covers an area of just 15 square miles. Once known as the 'Gibraltar of the East', it was a flourishing Portuguese colony from the 16th century. It was ceded to India in 1961. Diu Fort on the eastern end of the island dominates the town. It was built in 1535 when Portugal took control of Diu. From the fort it is possible to see the Church of St.Paul (above, centre left) which was built in 1610, although its impressive Gothic facade was rebuilt in 1807. It was also possible to see the Church of St.Thomas (below) which was built in 1598 with its museum of religious artifacts and stone inscriptions linked to the island's history. A quick dip in the sea from Nagoa Beach wasn't very enjoyable: the sea was warm but a bit mucky and the sand was grey and like mud. Despite the resort pool ponging of chlorine, it did feel a bit cleaner. Driving back from Diu town in a tuk-tuk we stopped at this extraordinary little Seashell Museum which is curated and stocked by a delightful man who has been all over the world collecting ... well, seashells. It was a real labour of love.

title: 35.Mumbai
text: India - 2007 Mumbai . A taxi to Diu airport and then a flight via Porbandar (birthplace of Mahatma Gandhi) to Mumbai. On our first morning we took a boat trip from the Gateway of India (Mumbai's most famous colonial monument) to Elephanta Island . Originally known as Gharapuri (the 'city of Ghara priests'), the island was renamed in the sixteenth century by the Portuguese in honour of the carved elephant they found at the port. On arrival at the island you are met by a dinky train and cool drink and souvenir stalls which line the way up the hill to the caves. Elephanta's impressive cave system was built (or, more strictly, dug) in the eighth century. Inside, the massive columns carved from solid rock, give the deceptive impression of being structural. A powerful 6m-high bust of Trimurti , the three-faced Shiva, who embodies the powers of creator, preserver and destroyer stands near a large lingam which is surrounded by coins and smouldering joss left by devotees. At the entrance to the cave is a panel of Nataraj , Shiva as the cosmic dancer. It was damaged by the Portuguese who, it is said used it for target practice. Shiva's face is rapt and, in one of his left hands, he removes the veil of ignorance. In the photo (left, below) Seán stands next to a panel showing Ravana shaking Kailas. High on the top of Malabar Hill , screened from prying eyes by an imposing wall and a dense curtain of vegetation, stand the seven Parsi Towers of Silence or dokhmas . The Parsis dispose of their dead by leaving the corpses on top of tall cylindrical enclosures for their bones to be picked clean by vultures. This ancient mortuary ritual was advocated by the prophet Zoroaster as a means of avoiding pollution of the four sacred elements (air, water, earth, and the holiest of them all, fire). We tried to visit the Towers by taxi but, despite almost making it to the top of the hill, we were turned back by the guards. Near Mahalakshmi Railway Station we saw the municipal dhobi ghats , a huge open-air laundry. Each morning, washing from all over Mumbai is brought here to be thrown into soapy piles and thumped by the resident dhobi wallahs in countless concrete tanks. The next day, after being aired, pressed, folded in newspaper and bound with cotton thread, the bundles are returned to their owners. A bizarre photo-opportunity. Our last evening in Mumbai found us in a splendid curry house with an Arsenal-supporting waiter who supplied us with cocktails as well as delicious food. A marvellous send off on our way back to the UK.

title: Bangkok Airport
text: Indo-China 2017 Bangkok Airport A few images while we change planes at Bangkok Airport. We're not actually in the "King Power" Lounge at Suvarnabhumi International Airport but the name was irresistible.

title: Cambodia Angkor Thom
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Angkor Thom It is hard to imagine any building bigger or more beautiful than Angkor Wat but, at Angkor Thom, the sum of the parts adds up to a greater whole. It is the gates that get your attention first, flanked by a monumental representation of the 'Churning of the Ocean of Milk', 54 demons and 54 gods engaged in an epic tug-of-war on the causeway. Each of the gates towers above the visitor, the magnanimous faces of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara staring out over the kingdom .

title: Cambodia Angkor Wat
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Angkor Wat The big one. Constructed over 37 years in the 12th century (ie: contemporary with Notre-Dame and Chartres Cathedrals), Angkor Wat is the Mt Olympus of the Hindu faith (if you pardon the mixed metaphor of Greek and Indian religions). The central tower is called Mt. Meru and the whole complex is supposed to represent the 'spatial universe' in miniature - the lower courtyards being the continents and the vast moat, the oceans. As a precursor to Wagnerian symbolism, the seven-headed 'naga' (mythical serpent) serves as a symbolic rainbow bridge for humans to reach the abode of the gods. However ... despite all that I felt slightly underwhelmed as I didn't feel any 'spirit of place'. Perhaps it was the hoards of tourists jostling for the best views or just the intense heat and humidity. Simply because it is the biggest religious site in the world, doesn't mean it is the best. We all know that size isn't everything. We returned here in the early evening to watch the sunset, and I was pleased to see a more human side to this vast and rather impersonal temple. Whole families of local Cambodians had replaced the snap-happy tourists, Buddhist monks took photos of each other and monkeys scavenged fruit from rubbish bins. And I was twice photo-bombed - once by Joan Thomson by the moat and once by a pussycat with Giulia Falsetti - both at sunset at Angkor Wat.

title: Cambodia Banteay Srei
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Banteay Srei Considered by many to be the jewel in the crown of Angkor temples due to the stunning three-dimensional carvings and pink hued stone, Banteay Srei (meaning Temple of the Goddess) dates from AD 967 and is one of the smaller sites at Angkor.

title: Cambodia Baphuon
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Baphuon Described as the 'world's largest jigsaw puzzle', Baphuon was being painstakingly being taken apart piece-by-piece and restored by archeologists before the civil war, but their records were destroyed during the Khmer Rouge regime leaving experts with 300,000 stones to put back in place. After years of research, this temple has been partially restored. On the western side, the retaining wall of the second level was fashioned, in the 16th century, into a reclining Buddha 60m in length .

title: Cambodia Bayon
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Bayon The 12th century Bayon is the mesmerising, if slightly mind-boggling, state temple of Jayavarman VII and epitomises the creative genius and inflated ego of Cambodia's most celebrated king. Its 54 gothic towers are famously decorated with 216 gargantuan smiling faces of Avalokiteshvara that bear more than a passing resemblance to the great king himself. These huge heads glare down from every angle, exuding power with a hint of humanity - precisely the blend required to hold sway over such a vast empire, ensuring the disparate and far-flung population yielded to the king's magnanimous will. The Bayon is decorated with 1.2km of extraordinary bas-reliefs incorporating more than 11,000 figures, depicting everyday life in 12th century Cambodia.

title: Cambodia Phnom Penh1
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Phnom Penh A stressful crossing from Vietnam over into Cambodia: our guide had to bribe the Vietnam border officials to process our exit visas in a 'timely fashion', we then had to trudge about a quarter of a mile in the blazing sun across No-Man's-Land overlooked by watch towers while dragging our suitcases and then, at the Cambodia border had to pay a further 'bribe' to enter the nation. Phnom Penh means the hill (phnom) of Lady Penh. Legend has it that in 1373 she found four Buddha statues floating in the Mekong and built this hill and pagoda to worship them. She was successful and now has all number of rather fetching (albeit camp) statues of various deities. Note especially the offerings of a stuffed pig's head, fresh meat placed in the mouths of the temple guardians and some enchanting temple maidens selling lotus flowers .

title: Cambodia Phnom Penh2
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Phnom Penh We also visited the stunning Royal Palace with its ornate gilding and flights-of-fancy roof lines. I felt I was starring in my very own version of The King and I . (And yes, I know that's set in Thailand). The palace was constructed after King Norodom relocated the royal capital from Oudong to Phnom Penh in the mid-19th century. It was built atop an old citadel called Banteay Kev. It faces towards the East and is situated at the Western bank of the cross division of the Tonle Sap and Mekong Rivers. s. Looking more like the original line-up of The Nolans, these mannequins display the daily dress colours of the ladies-in-waiting to the Queen. Male bodyguards are colour-coordinated too. I'm in the mood for dancing indeed .. .

title: Cambodia Phnom Penh3
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Phnom Penh At the Choeung Ek Genocidal Centre ('The Killing Fields of Pol Pot'), it's hard to comprehend the brutality that occured in this peaceful, shady former orchard (and previously a Chinese cemetery). Under the Pol Pot regime, however, over 20,000 people were killed here merely for being educated, from the professional classes or wearing spectacles. A newly-built memorial stupa brings it home, displaying more than 8,000 skulls of victims and their ragged clothes.

title: Cambodia Phnom Penh4
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Phnom Penh The Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum. This former high school in Phnom Penh was taken over by Pol Pot's security forces in 1975 and turned into a prison known as S-21 and was soon the largest centre of detention and torture in the country. Seán meets Chum Mey who is only one of seven survivors of the prison. He was spared from execution, following two years of torture, because of his skills as a mechanic and able to repair a typewriter. He witnessed the killing of his wife and young son. Like the Nazis, the Khmer Rouge were meticulous in keeping records of their barbarity. Each prisoner who passed through S-21 was photographed, sometimes before and after torture. The long corridors contain haunting photographs of the victims, their faces staring eerily from the past.

title: Cambodia Phnom Penh5
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Phnom Penh At the Frangipani Royal Sky Bar - in their lovely roof-top pool. Just the place for a delicious swim. Views over the Royal Palace Museum, which we visited yesterday, where they are landscaping the gardens. .. We come all the way to Cambodia, only to find the highlight of the menu is a "Big English Sausage". After three weeks of exotic flavours, we've gone for the bland option today with tofu burger & chips and ginger fried rice with pork. And some really healthy drinks. Not an artificial colour to be seen anywhere ...

title: Cambodia Phnom Penh6
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Phnom Penh Phnom Penh's Central Market was constructed in 1937 in the Art Deco style. It is in the shape of a dome with four arms branching out into vast hallways with countless stalls of goods and was designed by French architect Jean Desbois (1891-1971). When it first opened in 1937, it was said to be the biggest market in Asia. It has now been extensively renovated but the surrounding area is still shabby. . We were fascinated by the focus on "beauty" in the market. There are businesses here that export much of their supply of human hair to the African and Jewish markets. You won't recognise Philip with his hair extensions when you next see him.

title: Cambodia Roluos Group
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Bakong Temple Our first temple visit at Angkor, the Bakong Temple in the Roluos Group is the oldest dating from the 8th century. Built and dedicated to Shiva by Indravarman I, it is a representation of Mt. Meru and served as the city's central temple. Security at the whole Angkor site is a priority and we were each given a 3-day non-transferable pass to the Temple Complex.

title: Cambodia Siem Reap1
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Siem Reap We found this wonderful bar in the back streets of Siem Reap - Miss Wong Cocktail Bar - which carried us back to the chic of 1920s Shanghai. Gay-friendly and extremely popular with the well-heeled expat crowd .

title: Cambodia Siem Reap2
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Siem Reap Our final evening in Siem Reap before our flight home. We revisited our haunts in Pub Street and, while a 'cultural night' and an 'all-you-can-eat' buffet is normally something I would eschew, this was perfectly acceptable. (NB: job-seekers - they are still looking for extra members for the back row of the chorus) .. .

title: Cambodia Ta Prohm
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Ta Prohm Now seemingly better known for being the location where Angelina Jolie got her kit off and did the Tomb Raider thing, Ta Prohm is truly magnificent, its crumbling towers and walls locked in the slow muscular embrace of vast root systems. Dating from 1186, or to put it another way, when Henry II was on the English throne ie: before Richard the Lionheart. My favourite temple of them all.

title: Cambodia Terrace Elephants
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Terrace of the Elephants The 350m-long Terrace of the Elephants was used as a viewing stand for public ceremonies and served as a base for the king's audience hall. Try to imagine the grandeur of the Khmer Empire at its height, with infantry, cavalry, horse-drawn chariots and elephants parading across Central Square in a procession, pennants and standards aloft. Looking on is the god-king, shaded by multi-tiered parasols and attended by mandarins and handmaidens bearing gold and silver utensils. Meanwhile the Terrace of the Leper King dates from the 12th century and is a 7m-high platform on top of which stands a nude, but sexless, statue. The statue was called the "Leper King" because discolouration and moss growing on it was reminiscent of a person with leprosy, and also because it matched a Cambodian legend of an Angkor King, Yasovarman I, who had leprosy. The front retaining walls of the terrace are decorated with at least five tiers of meticulously executed carvings. On the day we visited, the whole site was swamped with armed guards as the President of Cambodia was paying a visit.

title: Cambodia Tonle Sap1
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Phnom Penh to Tonlé Sap On the road from Phnom Penh to Tonlé Sap Lake we stopped at this market. They sell the 'local delicacy' - deep fried insects: spiders, maggots (silkworm larvae), beetles, cockroaches, crickets and water snakes. All of which seemed absolutely disgusting and I wouldn't try any. In fact, it still makes me shudder when I think about it .

title: Cambodia Tonle Sap2
text: Indo-China 2017 Cambodia - Tonlé Sap Lake Tonlé Sap Lake is the largest freshwater lake in Southeast Asia and hosts one of the world’s most vibrant ecosystems, with massive numbers of many different species of wildlife which helped to sustain and grow the ancient Khmer civilisation. It is also well known for its local communities and their floating villages. The massive lake is as much as 250 km in length and 100 km across at its widest point, making it seem like an inland ocean because it is impossible to see the opposite shore from ground level. Surprisingly it is actually fairly shallow, with a maximum depth of only 10 metres. While the lake was a spectacular sight, we were slightly troubled by the power cable health and safety arrangements on our boat ...

title: Itinerary
text: Indo-China 2017 Indo-China itinerary - March / April 2017

title: Laos Luang Prabang1
text: Indo-China 2017 Laos - Luang Prabang Exotic night market in Luang Prabang where you can buy virtually anything ... ll in comparison ...

title: Laos Luang Prabang2
text: Indo-China 2017 Laos - Luang Prabang The unedifying spectacle of humble Buddhist monks receiving alms - while being photographed by Chanel-clad, well-heeled, iPad-toting Japanese, Korean, Chinese and, yes, western tourists. However, the saving grace is the cute puppy. Plus a few random (and hopefully not too predictable) photos of Luang Prabang. ll in comparison ...

title: Laos Luang Prabang3
text: Indo-China 2017 Laos - Luang Prabang The Sun Bears at the Tat Kuang Si Rescue Centre have been rescued from poachers who would sell them to traders in the vile bear-bile-business (pardon excessive alliteration) and are kept here in preference to releasing them to the same certain fate. ll in comparison ...

title: Laos Luang Prabang4
text: Indo-China 2017 Laos - Luang Prabang The fabulous multi-tiered Tat Kuang Si waterfalls tumble into azure-blue pools that are popular for swimming. ll in comparison ...

title: Laos Luang Prabang5
text: Indo-China 2017 Laos - Luang Prabang A super lunch, fresh coconut juice, a tuk-tuk ride, Lao coffee and alms-giving at a Buddhist Temple. ll in comparison ...

title: Laos Luang Prabang6
text: Indo-China 2017 Laos - Luang Prabang Some old world glamour, a great supper at fusion restaurant Tamarind , some trainee Buddhist monks and some street dancing on our last day in Laos. Off to Vietnam (Hanoi) tomorrow. ll in comparison ...

title: Laos Nong Khiaw1
text: Indo-China 2017 Laos - Nong Khiaw Following a flight and then a three hour drive we arrived at Nong Khiaw and our home (Phaxang Resort) for the next two nights. And what a beautiful sunset over the River Ou (tributary of the Mekong) at Muang Ngoi!

title: Laos Nong Khiaw2
text: Indo-China 2017 Laos - Nong Khiaw An all-day longboat trip to the villages of Sopjam and Muang Ngoi allowed us to see these lovely tranquil scenes. And a stop on the boat for lunch allowed us to visit a village with families of weavers. ll in

title: Laos Nong Khiaw3
text: Indo-China 2017 Laos - Nong Khiaw The Lao are keen to leave official notices in your rooms and their intent is pretty clear. But as if I would make love with anyone who was not my own wife ... After all that instruction we head off out for dinner where we try some of the Mekong River Weed which, actually, was quite tasty.

title: Laos Pak Ou Caves
text: Indo-China 2017 Laos - Pak Ou Caves Where the Nam Ou River meets the Mekong, there's no such thing as too many Buddhas. I like the one which makes my pot belly look small in comparison ... ll in comparison ...

title: Laos Vientiane1
text: Indo-China 2017 Laos - Vientiane Our first day in Laos on arrival in Vientiane. Sunset over the Mekong river, the statue of King Sisavang Vong (1904-1959) and the delicious scent of frangipani.

title: Laos Vientiane2
text: Indo-China 2017 Laos - Vientiane At Wat Si Muang. Our first visit to a temple - that of the Emerald Buddha. In the large sim (ordination hall) petitioners who can lift a stone copy of it from its pillow three times whilst kneeling are supposed to have their wishes granted. With our lovely travelling companion for the next three weeks - Joan Thomson - and our rather irritating guide Khamla Lorvanxay "La". Plus a gratuitous shot of some officials doing their exercises ...

title: Laos Vientiane2b
text: Indo-China 2017 Laos - Vientiane Built between 1819 and 1824 by Chao Anou, Wat Si Saket is believed to be Vientiane's oldest surviving temple. And it shows: this beautiful temple (with its thousands of Buddha figures) is in dire need of a facelift. We also met an artist selling his work. This man used to be an art teacher before the 'Vietnam War' which spilled over into Laos (Laos was secretly bombed by US forces under orders from Presidents Kennedy, Johnson and Nixon) forcing him to change his way of life.

title: Laos Vientiane3
text: Indo-China 2017 Laos - Vientiane At Pha That Luang. The Great Sacred Reliquary. Legend has it that Ashokan missionaries from India erected a Stupa here in the 3rd century BC to house a piece of the Buddha's breastbone. The monks have a magnificent hall in which to eat their lunch.

title: Laos Vientiane4
text: Indo-China 2017 Laos - Vientiane The rather incongruous sight of a concrete Victory Monument (Patuxai Laos - built in 1969) with ornate ceilings which would not look out of place at Versailles. Built with cement donated by the USA intended for the construction of the new airport but which never quite made it there .. .

title: Laos Vientiane5
text: Indo-China 2017 Laos - Vientiane Fabulous restaurant where we (Seán, me and our travelling companion Joan) ate today - together with beautiful water garden at the front. We didn't, however, try number 7 on the menu. And then, after a lovely supper, we are off back to the hotel. Only problem is we can't remember where we are staying ...

title: Vietnam Ben Tre1
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Bên Tre Delightful 82 year old gent who served us fruit on our wanderings through the backwaters yesterday. He tells us he has 8 children and 13 grandchildren. He must have lived through a heck of a lot of history here in Vietnam. We also stopped at a sweatshop where they were making snazzy football shoes for Nike. The temperature was boiling in the workshop (look how frazzled I look) and the workers were probably paid a pittance to make the shoes which are then sold expensively back home. Plus some photos of our home stay location and our dinner, fried elephant ear fish ( gourami ). It's always nice to meet your dinner before you eat them ...

title: Vietnam Ben Tre2
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Bên Tre Viewers with a delicate disposition, look away now ... Looking more like a medieval charnel house, these offal and meat stalls in Bên Tre market would not look out of place in a slasher movie. I've never felt more like converting to vegetarianism (and you know that really means something to a confirmed carnivore like me). The final touch was the Madame Defarge-like creature sleeping in her hammock above the slabs of meat below . Plus a surprise cake on the eve of my birthday ...

title: Vietnam Chu Chi Tunnels
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Chu Chi Tunnels Beginning in the late 1940s, the Chu Chi Tunnels were originally dug by the Viet Minh during the war against the French. Extended by the Viet Cong in the 1960s, the tunnel system stretched from Saigon to the Cambodian border and enabled the VC to mount surprise attacks on the US military and then to disappear into hidden trapdoors without trace. The network, parts of which were several storeys deep, included storage facilities, weapon factories, field hospitals and kitchens. There is also a gun range attached where tourists can shell out a small fortune (you pay per bullet) to fire genuine AK47s and machine guns. The guards looked bored and disinterested. The tunnels we visited have been enlarged to accommodate tourists (1.2m high, 80cm across and unlit) although they are still a tight, airless and claustrophobic squeeze. I forced myself to go through one of the tunnels (30m in length or so) and emerged feeling disorientated and sweaty at the other end.

title: Vietnam Halong Bay1
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Halong Bay The depressing fact that the whole world is in thrall to the Chinese Yuan. Acres of pristine beachfront have now been turned into a concrete monstrosity - a theme park for Vietnam's northern neighbours who comprise 60% of the tourists. It surprised even our tour guide. This is the view from our hotel bedroom ... ll in comparison ...

title: Vietnam Halong Bay2
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Halong Bay A misty morning in Halong Bay meant we got a slightly more 'atmospheric' experience than expected - but stunning nonetheless. And a happy post-lunch soda-pop photo with Paula Eddery, Dawn Kendall, Seán and me. ll on ...

title: Vietnam Halong Bay3
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Halong Bay Be careful of what you wish for ... This garishly-lit cave in Halong Bay (Hang Sung Sot, nicknamed the 'Surprise Cave') includes a pink-lit rock phallus unsurprisingly regarded as a fertility symbol. The locals charmingly call it the 'Cock Rock' ... Plus some crazy Korean ladies on Titop Island and what looks like a Michael Jackson lookalike. ll in comparison ...

title: Vietnam Halong Bay4
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Halong Bay Some more bonkers, incomprehensible (and, frankly, vulgar) signs and labels. ll in comparison ...

title: Vietnam Hanoi1
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Hanoi A late night taxi ride into Hanoi from the airport, our hotel room which appears to double as a fish tank and a charming local bar. The next morning we see what appears to be an Eduardo Paolozzi sculpture in a lake: this is in fact a B52 bomber which was downed into this lake (Huu Tiep) in central Hanoi in December 1972. And stayed there ... ll in comparison ...

title: Vietnam Hanoi2
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Hanoi At the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum. Apparently voted sixth most ugly building in the world, I thought it looked just like ... er, a mausoleum. Plus I find a uniformed friend and Seán buys a hat. ll in comparison ...

title: Vietnam Hanoi3
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Hanoi Downtown Hanoi. I love people-watching. ll in comparison ...

title: Vietnam Hanoi4
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Hanoi The gaudy Presidential Palace (with visiting monks), plus graduation celebrations at the Temple of Literature, the Vietnamese bank note which features the Temple and two musical old birds. ll in comparison ...

title: Vietnam Hanoi5
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Hanoi The Hoa Lo Prison (ironically nicknamed the 'Hanoi Hilton' by US POWs during the American War) is a thought-provoking site. Most of the exhibits relate to the prison's use up to the mid-1950s focusing on the Vietnamese struggle for independence from France. A gruesome relic is the French guillotine used to behead Vietnamese revolutionaries. There are also displays featuring American pilots who were incarcerated there - including US Senator John McCain. ll in comparison ...

title: Vietnam Hanoi6
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Hanoi Great dinners (BBQ seafood and beef hotpot) and lashings of beer with lovely new friends on our last evening in Hanoi. ll in comparison ...

title: Vietnam Ho Chi Minh1
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Ho Chi Minh City Who'd have thought it at the Mile High Club in Saigon. Birthday drinks on the 52nd floor (Saigon Skydeck) of the Bitexco Financial Tower with Claire, Paula, Dawn, Joan and Monica plus Ho Chi Minh City's very own Peters & Lee. It's a long way down ...

title: Vietnam Ho Chi Minh2
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Ho Chi Minh City Some gorgeous tourists (us) by a statue of Ho Chi Minh, Saigon Opera House, a Virgin Mary statue at the rather dull replica of Notre Dame Cathedral with a weird pink (?) pigeon, Saigon Central Post Office (designed by Gustave Eiffel) and a pair of brides to be - one smiling, one grumpy! Saigon has completely transformed since the end of the Vietnam War. No more so than the US Embassy where, on 29 April 1975, the last few American evacuees were hustled up a ladder on the roof of the Embassy to a waiting helicopter while US Marines cruelly kicked off any desperate South Vietnamese citizens who were also trying to flee. I remember seeing these tragic scenes on TV when I was a teenager. Ironically the Yankie Dollar has returned with a vengeance: the new blue building in my photo is the turbo-expensive Hyatt Regency Hotel.

title: Vietnam Ho Chi Minh3
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Ho Chi Minh City Stunning James Bond -style interiors at the Reunification Palace. Presumably paid for with US money, it was in fact designed by Paris-trained Vietnamese architect Ngo Viet Thu. It was commissioned by President Ngo Dinh Diem who was so unpopular that his own air force bombed the previous palace in 1962 in an attempt to kill him. This new palace was finished in 1966 (complete with bomb-proof bunker in the basement) but Diem did not get to see his dream house as he was assassinated by his own troops in 1963. It's a stunning building nonetheless - a perfect example of mid-60s moderne design.

title: Vietnam Ho Chi Minh4
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Ho Chi Minh City This could have been Dr No's hideout designed by Ken Adam but is in fact Saigon's (sorry, HCMC's) Presidential Palace. Magnificent. The first Communist tanks to arrive in Saigon crashed through the wrought-iron gates on 30 April 1975 (picture below) in a dramatic scene recorded by journalists and shown round the world .

title: Vietnam Hoi An1
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Hoi An Classic views of this graceful and historic town. Once a major port, it has benefitted from the Thu Bon River silting up in the late 19th century so ships could no longer access the town's docks and therefore retaining its easygoing provincial demeanour and harmonious old-town character. It was also virtually untouched during the American War thanks to the co-operation of both sides. It

title: Vietnam Hoi An2
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Hoi An Exquisite 18th century houses in Hoi An Historic Centre. Although the town is prone to flooding it is beautifully preserved and reeking with atmosphere. There's nothing quite like a dusty old museum (and some awkwardly dressed mannequins) for a giggle. No wonder he looks miserable: his wife has a broken arm and a moustache ... The Vinh Hung Hotel features in the 2002 film A Quiet American featuring Michael Caine. And on the Japanese Covered Bridge we found a shrine to Saint Sammy and his monkey friend.

title: Vietnam Hoi An3
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Hoi An Imagine Jack Cardiff's 1968 Girl on a Motorcycle (starring Marianne Faithfull and Alain Delon) remade for the Vietnam market. Not so much a case of tight-fitting, body-hugging leather as one-size-fits-all polka-dot plastic tablecloth ... Another delicious lunch in old town Hoi An - this time at Vy's Market Restaurant. And I didn't realise that Brian Blessed was so popular here ... Gordon's alive !!

title: Vietnam Hoi An4
text: Indo-China 2017 Vietnam - Hoi An This temple complex at My Son (pronounced Me Sun ) was active as a religious centre between the 4th and 13th centuries (ie: the longest period of development of any monuments in Southeast Asia) was dedicated to the Cham kings associated with divinities such as Shiva. At one point in their history, the domes of some of the towers were covered with gold.
